Mr. Speaker, the motion to limit debate on Bill C-70 which will deindex family allowances by 3 per cent is a cheap attempt by the Government to suppress debate and keep the following facts from the public. A 3 per cent deindexation of family allowances is an unfair attack on children, families and women and particularly on single-parent mothers. Family allowance deindexing will not be offset by changes to the child tax credit and even the poorest families will be worse off by 1990. Cut-backs to children will amount to $600 million by 1990 which can be added to the increased sales taxes, excise taxes and income taxes already imposed on families by this Budget. This places an extraordinary burden on middle and low-income families.
While cutting the family allowance to save for the deficit and increasing taxes on families as well, the Government at the same time somehow finds $8 billion to give to the oil companies, $1 billion to bail out the banks and has increased tax loopholes for the rich. We believe that this is immoral, inequitable and unfair.
In closing, I say again on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we call on the Government, in the name of fairness, to reverse its position on Bill C-70. We call on the Government to index family allowances fully and to show that it cares for Canada's children, women and families.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
that Bill C-73, an Act to validate certain ordinances of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this morning I ask Hon. Members to turn their attention to a matter concerning residents of Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I am introducing new legislation, the Condominium Ordinance Validation Act, which will remove a conflict between territorial and federal laws that has held back the construction of new condominium housing in the North.
It is a pleasure to note that all Parties in the House, through a unanimous resolution of the Standing Committee on Indian
Affairs and Northern Development, have already given their support to this Bill which validates territorial ordinances. I might say, parenthetically, that I received a telephone call from the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) on the weekend who has a concern, which may be peripheral to the Bill, that he would like to raise in committee. Aside from that, we have had excellent co-operation, which speaks well for all those people involved, particularly the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) who spearheaded the effort to resolve the matter.
The federal legislation with which the existing territorial condominium ordinances are in conflict is the Land Titles Act of 1894. It is long forgotten in most of Canada. It applied to northern and western territories which Canada acquired after Confederation. As the western provinces came into being, they passed their own legislation dealing with land ownership and real estate. However, the old law, amended from time to time, that is to say, the law of 1894, remained in force for Canada's northern territories. Unfortunately, the technicalities of the old law no longer fit today's circumstances. In fact, they hold back the introduction of new kinds of home building and home ownership.
Today, Yellowknife and other northern communities face severe housing problems. Mr. Speaker, you may have seen press reports on the special committee which the Northwest Territories Legislative Assembly set up on housing indicating that the committee found the situation in the Northwest Territories to be no less than a crisis. A few months ago the Mayor of Yellowknife, His Worship Mayor Don Sian, explained to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development what the housing situation means in everyday life to northern people. Of the larger centres in the North, the City of Yellowknife has almost one-quarter the population of the Northwest Territories. Many more people are moving there to work at mining and exploration, at new head offices, in the Government, in the new regional hospital and so on. However, when it comes to finding a place to rent, they can almost forget it. The vacancy rate in Yellowknife is zero. I have heard that a single apartment will often have a waiting list of over 100 people.
As for buying a house, Mayor Sian estimated a housing shortfall in the immediate future of at least 250 units. He explained that available housing falls into two ranges, both of which are expensive compared with the South because of transportation costs for materials and other difficulties of building in the North, particularly as a consequence of the climate. A trailer on a privately owned lot will set one back $75,000 to $95,000, and a new single family housing unit of modest size will cost $160,000.
The Mayor added:
Yellowknife is a fairly young community and for a young family to get together the down payment to move into a single family home of.. . $160,000 is quite simply beyond their means.
Obviously condominiums do not provide all the answers. However, they will probably help fill the gap between the trailer and the single family house and provide private housing
September 26, 1985

at a relatively reasonable cost. Condominiums would seem to make especially good sense in places like Yellowknife, where the rocky Canadian shield makes it difficult to run in services such as water and sewage. When multiple units can share services, it cuts down the costs.
The legislators who wrote the Land Titles Act dealt only with conditions which they saw in their own time, in the 1890s-an owner had a piece of land with a building on it, and that was how land titles worked. The Act made no provisions for title to condominiums. In 1969 in the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, and in 1968 in Yukon, ordinances were passed respecting condominiums. A later opinion by the federal Department of Justice found that the ordinances could not be fully effective because of the deficiency in the Land Titles Act respecting title registration. This put the legal registration of titles to condominiums in doubt. The result was and is that no condominiums have been built in the Northwest Territories. Some buildings built with that intention ended up as regular rental units. Developers who would otherwise build condominiums today, and their financial backers, are reluctant because of the uncertainty surrounding the security of condominium titles.
The territorial and federal Governments have been concerned with this problem for several years. The previous federal Government twice tried to pass Bills addressing the issue, but they fell by the wayside. That delay in addressing the matter has made it all the more urgent. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic highlighted the matter by putting forward a Private Member's Bill, Bill C-214, affecting the Northwest Territories only. I am pleased, after discussions with him, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), who is also the Hon. Member for Yukon, and the Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk), to build on his initiative. Therefore, I offer a Government Bill which will resolve the matter for both the Northwest Territories and Yukon.
On May 28 of this year the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development offered its unanimous support for such legislation in these words:
In accordance with its Order of Reference of Friday, December 21, 1984, in relation to the subject matter of Bill C-214, an Act to validate the Northwest Territories Condominium Ordinance, your committee has held one meeting and has heard the testimony of Gary MacDougall, Registrar of Land Titles, Don Sian, Mayor of the City of Yellowknife and Dave Nickerson, M.P. and has agreed to recommend the following:
That the House of Commons support the early enactment of legislation which would have the effect of deeming valid for all purposes the territorial ordinances dealing with condominiums and of making valid everything that has been done to date under the territorial ordinances.
The legislation I propose to you will do exactly what the standing committee recommended. And besides the support of the standing committee, this action has the support of the City of Yellowknife, of the N.W.T. Association of Municipalities, of the Yellowknife Chamber of Commerce, and of MLA's and the Territorial Governments themselves. This is one of those rare Bills that everyone supports. It will not cost the federal Government a penny. It has no effect on native land claims or
Condominium Ordinance Validation Act Crown lands; it only deals with property already privately owned, making it possible to put up condominiums rather than single-owner buildings.
It is a Bill that will bring more affordable houses to many families. It will protect the interest of condominium owners and it will help the northern economy. It will not solve all the housing problems overnight, but it should be a big help.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I recommend consideration of the Bill to all Hon. Members.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my seat today and give support to this legislation which should help to resolve the urgent needs for affordable housing in many northern communities.
I want to indicate to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) that this Bill being presented in the House of Commons today is a reflection of a process of devolution that began years ago. I am glad to see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is following through with that same process of devolution to give to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon more and more power given more priority to local input that to central agencies, such as the federal Government.
My personal thanks goes to Members, on behalf of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), who unfortunately is unable to be here and whose notes I am using. I acknowledge the work he has done on the Standing Committee of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, as well the work which the standing committee did to facilitate the passage of this legislation we see here today.
I have some general comments on the thrust of the Bill. While this Bill deals with what might be considered a relatively small issue on the national agenda, I wish to draw to the attention of the House the significance of what we are actually doing. The Bill before us should give us cause to reflect on the nature between the Territorial Governments and the federal Government. The Governments of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are still, even today, subject to much federal dominance, and I think the process that began in the last several years and is speeding up will go a long way toward giving them more and more powers.
This Bill itself resolves a conflict in jurisdiction. It will allow the Territorial Governments to proceed with legislation legally which they enacted over 15 years ago. We are dealing here with an outdated federal Act conflicting with modern reality.
Parliament is being called upon to deal with condominiums in the Territories because Parliament has an overriding jurisdiction over the Territories. Territorial ordinances are subject to overriding federal legislation. I hope the Minister can bring forward legislation that will allow the Territorial Governments to establish their own Acts for Land Titles and enable those same Territorial Governments to repeal the Land Titles Act themselves.

September 26, 1985
Condominium Ordinance Validation Act
Devolution seems to be a very arduous task. Many interests have to be taken into account. I presume that lack of consensus probably inhibited the implementation of old Bill C-52, which supposedly was going to deal with this problem of housing in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
However, I urge the Government to proceed expeditiously where there is agreement among northerners to transfer more and more responsibilities to the Territorial Governments.
In addition, I want to pay tribute not only to members of that committee but to a number of other individuals who, I believe, were instrumental in assisting in obtaining quick passage of this Bill. Some Members, among whom I am sure is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), would agree with me that even in as small a Bill as this, because of the way in which the complexities of government machinery work here in Ottawa, we lost this season's building time. It is unfortunate that this Bill could not have been passed, for instance, in May, allowing the Territorial Governments to go ahead with construction this season. That is no fault of the Minister, Mr. Speaker. It is the fault, basically, of the machinery of Government in getting Bills onto the floor of the House of Commons.
The Minister has outlined the specifics of the Bill. Let me point out that the Mayor of the City of Yellowknife appeared before the committee and testified, for example, that his city has a zero per cent vacancy rate. A trailer on a privately owned lot costs from $75,000 to $95,000. A newer single family unit costs between $140,000 to $160,000. Very few Canadians understand the cost of doing business in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Things that we take for granted in the southern part of Canada are not taken for granted by the residents of the two territorial areas. Believe me, one can understand why special tax considerations have to be given to people living in the Territories. Without special tax concessions, it is beyond me how they could make ends meet.
Housing is clearly out of reach for most of the people in the territorial areas. Condominiums could fill a very important but intermediate gap in the housing market. I want to pay some tribute to the Hon. Member for the Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) who was instrumental in bringing this problem before the committee.
Without taking up the time of the House, the Bill, its intent and its direction have the full support of the Liberal Party. I welcome the fact that we are finally able to deal with this legislation in such an expeditious manner.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I am pleased to indicate that we are prepared to deal with this Bill in a expeditious manner.
As has been pointed out, Bill C-73 is designed to enable condominiums to be built, sold and owned in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Basically it is a technical Bill, but it is a technicality we should not be dealing with in this House. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon should have full power to deal with this matter in their own Legislatures.
Amending the Land Titles Act will authorize the condominium Acts in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
While we are glad to give our consent to the speedy passage of this Bill, we also want to emphasize that housing is in crisis across Canada and particularly in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and in Indian communities across Canada, the areas for which the Minister has responsibility.
It is interesting that this past spring a Northwest Territories housing study pointed out that lack of housing was so severe throughout the North that up to 18 people are having to share three bedroom homes in some Inuit communities. Many of the Government's 4,000 rental units did not meet health and safety standards. People in more affluent communities, such as Yellowknife, are forced to camp out in shacks, tents or in the backs of tractor trailers during the long winters owing to the lack of rental units. The few two bedroom apartments that occasionally become available cost up to $1,100 a month.
It is especially important to note that the committee has warned that the desperate housing problem is most likely related to the dramatic increase in spousal assaults, family breakdowns and the dropping out of high school students throughout the North. In other words, when we look at the question of housing we are not simply dealing with an isolated physical situation. We are dealing with a dimension of the total situation facing people in the north. The crisis in housing stimulates crises in other areas of social life there as well. The possibility of condominiums may open the way for some people. Others, however, may need rental accommodation, and a 1983-1984 survey in Yellowknife by the Government of the Northwest Territories Bureau of Statistics indicated that of 1208 rental units 703 were leased by the Government of the Northwest Territories and 505 were leased privately. There is a vacancy rate of zero. The average rent in December of 1984 for a one-bedroom apartment was $613 and for a two-bedroom apartment was $773. This represented a 10 per cent increase from December of 1983.
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), the housing critic for the New Democratic Party, pointed out that there is one concern that he has with this Bill as it stands, and that is, that it may endanger the 505 private rental units in Yellowknife. As alderman in Toronto when he worked with the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) when that Minister was the Mayor of Toronto, he and the Minister became very concerned that a number of rental units were converted to condominiums, which forced people out of rental units and so they had nowhere to go.
Between 1969 and 1985, 1799 rental units were converted to condominiums in the City of Toronto. The present Minister, as Mayor of Toronto, led the City Council in establishing a policy which blocked conversion as long as vacancy was less than 2 per cent. The Hon. Member for Spadina suggests that the Condominium Acts of the Northwest Territories and Yukon should be amended so as to prohibit the conversion of rental units to condominium so long as there is a rental shortage.
September 26, 1985

Referral of this to committee will, of course, give the opportunity for the committee to discuss this with the Governments of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories.
I would like to make just a few comments about the situation on native housing across Canada. This is a longstanding problem, one that the Minister inherited from previous Governments and which has been increasing over a number of years. The backlog of new houses required has been estimated at a conservative figure of between 10,000 and 11,000. That has been the same for a number of years. Some other estimates state that that backlog is as high as 17,000.
The last federal census had some interesting figures on native housing across Canada. It pointed out that nearly one-quarter of Indian dwellings have more than one person per room and that the percentage of Indian dwellings which had more than one person per room was just over nine times that of all other dwellings in Canada. Nearly one-half of Indian dwellings in the Northwest Territories had more than one person per room. It pointed out that nearly one-fifth of all Indian dwellings need major repairs, almost three times that of all other dwellings in Canada. Among Indian dwellings, the Northwest Territories had the highest percentage, 28 per cent, in need of major repairs. The census also pointed out that one-third of Indian homes lacked a central heating system. The percentage of Indian dwellings which lacked a central heating system was almost four times that of all other dwellings in Canada. Just over one-half of Indian dwellings in Yukon had no central heating. Close to one-half of Indian dwellings in Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories did not have central heating. Nearly one-fifth of Indian dwellings lacked a bathroom and the percentage of Indian dwellings which had no bathroom was just over 15 times that of all other dwellings in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, these figures from the latest census indicate that Indian housing is a national disgrace and I urge the Minister to make strong representation to his Cabinet to ensure that attention is focused on this issue this coming year. We cannot allow this kind of disgraceful situation to continue in a country that prides itself, as Canada does, as being a modern and a progressive nation.
We have had continued representation from Indian communities about the lack of proper infrastructure. The Indian community of Tyendinaga in southern Ontario has for years been waging a battle to try to get decent water and sewage in a new subdivision area that they have because they fear that the present arrangements are very likely to lead to a serious health risk. It is interesting that when the present Minister was the Minister responsible for health and welfare in 1979 in the Clark Government he appointed Chief Justice Berger to look at the whole question of Indian health at the time. One of the recommendations of Chief Justice Berger pointed to this central situation of Indian housing and said that that was absolutely crucial in terms of Indian health and that when people are crowded together there is no possibility of their having a decent life or a decent community life.

This again goes back to the findings of the Northwest Territories housing situation, that when you have bad housing you have an increase in family violence, an increase in a great many social problems. Yet this summer we saw a cut-back of $455,000 to Operations Beaver, a co-operative project of Canadian churches for the past number of years which has a very good track record of working with Indian communities, working with Indian young people and young people from other parts of Canada and indeed other parts of the world in constructing housing on Indian reserves and also some off-reserve housing. Yet this group was cut back by $455,000.
Also this summer the Ekos study was released, which had been commissioned by the Department of Indian Affairs, and it confirmed the sort of statistics that I read from the latest census. It said that 47 per cent of all Indian housing is substandard. It indicated that our past mistakes are coming home to roost and I regret that the present Minister is having to pick up the pieces from mistakes that have been made by past Governments. I want to emphasize that he has that responsibility to pick up those pieces and to make sure that something is done. The Ekos study pointed out that 15 per cent of the houses built as late as 1983, two years ago, are substandard simply because the financing for those houses was substandard. Indian people have repeatedly raised problems with the whole question of funding, and the funding delays often mean that it is impossible for them to get their programs in place, to get their material in place in time to meet the short construction season. This summer the Minister promised some $600,000 to the Dene people for housing. The Dene are now being told that this $600,000 is being given for more general purposes. I urge the Minister to make that $600,000 available specifically for housing so that the Dene people in the Northwest Territories can meet their housing needs.
I wanted to lay all of these concerns before the House of Commons because I think it is very important that we be aware of this disgraceful and tragic situation. I know the Minister is aware of the situation. I hope that he will fight with all his strengh to get a decent program from the Cabinet so that one year from now, we will be able to report substantial progress in this situation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 wonder if I might have the consent of the House to put a question to the Hon. Member who just spoke? I recognize that it is not normal procedure, but there are two matters of fact which were raised on which 1 simply wanted to ask a question and seek the Hon. Member's views.

Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would associate myself with many of the remarks made by the Hon. Member with respect

September 26, 1985
Condominium Ordinance Validation Act
to the standard of housing in Canada and with respect to the report which he discussed at length, a report with which I am intimately familiar. I am looking forward to making some changes in it this year which I will be presenting to the Cabinet and the standing committee of the House.
There were two matters that the Hon. Member raised. I think it is important to understand the way we are approaching housing which is that Indian communities are now able to determine on their own how money ought to be spent. The Hon. Member's first point dealt with Operation Beaver and his second one with money flowing to the Dene.
I will put a question to the Hon. Member and ask him to offer his views. Does the Hon. Member appreciate that housing selections are done through the community or the band itself? In the past, the federal Government gave money to organizations, which then took the money to Indian communities. I want to know whether or not the Hon. Member feels that the process by which housing operates according to the choice of the community is, in his view, an appropriate way of doing things.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, certainly the communities themselves should make the basic determination of the way in which they will do things. However, the fact is that some $455,000 was cut from the housing allocation to Operation Beaver. I would be interested to know where the money cut from Operation Beaver went.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having understood that point of view, I would ask the Hon. Member if he is aware that the only reason the allocation did not go to Operation Beaver was that it went elsewhere. There was no general cut made. The money did not go to Operation Beaver because, at that point, Operation Beaver did not have sufficient requests from Indian communities.

Mr. Speaker, I was not aware of that particular problem but I appreciate the Minister's assurance that no absolute cut was made. In fact, I hope that there has been an addition to the budget.
The Minister also raised the question of funding to the Dene. My understanding is that the Minister made a direct commitment of $600,000 to the Dene for housing needs, but instead that money is now being made available under the recently announced Human Resource Development Strategy Program rather than specifically for housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask a further question? Is the Hon. Member aware that housing for the Dene in the Northwest Territories is primarily a responsibility of the Government of the Northwest Territories and that in housing matters we deal through that particular Government? Second, would it not be in line with his own views that when giving money to communities, it is much better for them to have the choice as to how the money is spent rather than having the federal Government directing them?

Mr. Speaker, again the Minister might be quite right in saying that housing is the specific responsibility of the Government of the Northwest Territories. However, I am under the impression, and the Minister can deny this if he wants, that the Minister made a specific commitment of $600,000 to the Dene people for housing, money which is not forthcoming at the present time. Rather, $600,000 has been made available for other purposes.
The Minister knows that Indian communities across Canada have a large agenda of needs and that the needs are many, varied and serious. Housing is one of those needs, but it is only one of those needs. Promising $600,000 specifically for housing and then making it available for a more general economic development program means that the specific housing needs in the Dene communities, needs which the Minister acknowledges are very serious, will not necessarily be met. Again I urge the Minister to make at least $600,000 available specifically for Dene housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is my last question. I appreciate the patience of Members of the House. Would the Hon. Member not agree that the most appropriate way for the federal Government to deal with housing in the North is in conjunction with the Territorial Government? Second, is he not aware that our particular role in these matters is one of providing funding for Indian communities but allowing them to choose where they would like to put the money?

Mr. Speaker, the points the Minister makes are quite valid. In the Northwest Territories it is appropriate for housing programs to be designed through the Government of the Northwest Territories. The point is that when the Minister was speaking to the Dene Assembly, he made a commitment of $600,000. The Minister shakes his head and denies that he made that commitment.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Not for housing, for housing-related matters.
The point is that quite apart from the best way in which funds should be allocated, when a specific commitment is made, I believe that that specific commitment should be followed through.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasant duty for me to speak to Bill C-73 today, a Bill which the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development requested us to put forward. As most Hon. Members may be aware, one of the first things that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) did was to travel north to meet with and listen to northerners. I would like to take a few moments to pay tribute to the Minister.
The Minister is a person who listens. He is someone who gets right into the fray and wants to see firsthand the experiences of the people for whom he is responsible. He wants to see how they are living and the conditions under which they live. He wants to see what he can do to change those conditions.
September 26, 1985

The Minister is a people person, one who cares and has seen firsthand the problems that native people are experiencing.
I will continue in this brief tribute to the Minister by saying that he is a Minister who is acquiring a knowledge and expertise of our vast North not only in a formal way through books and meetings but by getting out and meeting with the people and learning from firsthand experience. I think it important that the House know about it and that the people of Canada are made aware of this extraordinary Minister who has these extra-curricular activities. I wish to pay tribute to him. He is a person who listens to the northerners. Not only does he listen to them, he acts. It is one thing to listen but another to act. He does both.
My Minister found that all the people of the North are very much aware that they are on the verge of an exciting moment, a moment in which history and destiny will meet. The people with whom he met are, in a very sophisticated and politically mature fashion, trying to deal with a number of needs. Housing was identified as an area which required immediate attention. At the urging of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), the Mayor of Yellowknife told the standing committee what the situation means in human terms. When we talk about legislation in the House, or when we talk about it anywhere, it should be in human terms, in terms of how if affects people. His Worship Mayor Sian estimated that there is a housing shortfall in the immediate future of at least 250 units. If we said that there was a housing shortfall in Metropolitan Toronto of some 250 units, that would not bother us too much. However, when we speak about a housing shortage in the City of Yellowknife, a comparatively small city, then we are talking about a very serious matter.
On May 28, 1985, members of the committee unanimously requested that the House take early action on a Bill to amend the Land Titles Act, the purpose being to allow construction of condominiums in Yukon and the Northwest Territories. What has been introduced is legislation which will do just that. In pushing for change, Hon. Members had in mind at that time that condominiums could provide reasonably priced housing to ease this terrible shortage in the North.
In our own time, condominiums have, of course, become popular. They are popular in southern Canada because of their cost. The tremendous cost of servicing land today has continued to sky-rocket. If we think the cost of servicing land in southern Canada is expensive, then we should go to the North and see what it is like there. By sharing costs and services among all the owners in a multiple unit, builders can provide private ownership, generally speaking, at a lower cost. Condominiums make particularly good sense in northern centres, in places such as Yellowknife.
I am perhaps one of the privileged people in Canada since I have had an opportunity to visit our Far North on a number of occasions. I travelled this summer with a colleague of mine and we spent some time in the North. I have been in Yellowknife on a number of occasions. I have seen firsthand the rocky

Condominiums allow builders to cut down the costs by sharing them among a number of buyers. Developers and their financial backers who would otherwise have built condominiums have held back. They have done this because of the technicality which prevents a condominium owner from registering his or her title.
In the Northwest Territories, a few builders who started to put up condominiums ended by using them as rental units because of the problems with titles. I know this has caused some concern. Last year, the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories set up a special committee on housing, which found no less than a crisis. The special committee put forward 82 specific recommendations with respect to housing which gives Hon. Members an idea of the amount of concern regarding northern housing. As for opposition, we have heard none so far. The proposal will only affect property which is already in private hands. It will have no effects on Crown lands or native land claims.
Besides his other energetic work to bring this matter to parliamentary attention, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, put forward a Private Member's Bill, Bill C-214, to amend the law for the Northwest Territories only. In discussion with the Hon. Member, and others, the Government put its weight behind a similar but broader Bill for both the Northwest Territories and Yukon. It was to speed up passage of that Bill that the standing committee gave its unanimous support for early action. Today, the Bill is in our hands.
Perhaps it is unnecessary to say more except to thank all Members from each side of the House, those Members who have spoken today, as well as those Members who worked in committee, for moving this matter along so quickly.
In the future, the federal Government will play what I think will be a diminishing role in the administration of northern affairs. We are prepared to give the Territories more responsibility. The Minister has committed himself to giving them more responsibility, as has the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney). How quickly, though, depends in part on the wishes of the Territorial Governments themselves.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has spoken often of his desire to see northerners, through their Territorial Governments, take on greater responsibilities for the decisions which affect their daily lives. This stems from a genuine belief that the role of Government can often be most effectively carried out when it is closest to those most affected by its decisions. It recognizes that the federal Government in Ottawa, however well intentioned, cannot be as sensitive to many of the needs and priorities of northerners as are their own Territorial and local Governments. In many areas, the federal Government is anxious to see a devolution, with which the Minister agrees, toward more participation and a greater degree of responsibility at the territorial level.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in response to the remarks made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) who is one of the Ministers I most admire in the Cabinet-
Hear, hear!

-if he is still in the Cabinet. According to The Globe and Mail of today, all the Ministers in Cabinet will be gone by certain dates and only the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be left if the Government continues to receive ministerial resignations.
I note it is this Minister who is bringing forward this Bill with respect to condominiums. I know he is the one Yuppie Minister in the House, a young urban professional-maybe not so young anymore. Perhaps we should call him a Muppie. He is from Rosedale where there are a great many condominiums. It is somewhat ironic that he brings forward a Bill to aid in condominium construction in the North.
I understand why the Bill is being brought forward. It has to do with the technicalities of the law in the territories and the difficulties with respect to condominium development. The reason I rise today is not to tackle my friend and get into debate with him, as I like to do, or even to talk about Rosedale. The fact is that I happen to have lived in Yellowknife for a couple of years. It did not stunt my growth-I can see the Minister smiling. At least, it did not stunt my physical growth. My spiritual growth was enhanced by living in Yellowknife for a couple of years and by being a member of the bar of the Northwest Territories. That entitles me, I suppose, to practise law from Yellowknife right up to Eureka.
I would like to say a couple of things so the Minister and his Department can flag them, although I may be a bit out of date and perhaps the Minister will dismiss the suggestion. When I was in Yellowknife, housing was also difficult to obtain. I heard my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), speak about the scarcity of native housing and the fact that the scarcity of non-native housing was quite incredible. There is a lot of Government housing in Yellowknife. When I was there, that was what most of the housing was. There was always the feeling around town that there were a lot of Government houses standing empty at a time when people were trying to get housing. Five and six people were living in a two-bedroom house which they rented at an exhorbitant price and there was a lot of Government housing just sitting around empty. So I ask the Minister to talk to his bureaucrats. The bureaucrats in Yellowknife were very helpful and I am not criticizing them, but it is easy to get into a situation where a Government just leaves houses empty. I would ask the Minister to take a look at the possibility of providing some of that Government housing on a lease basis to non-government people. I know there have to be some houses empty because people rotate in Yellowknife. They usually stay
up there for a couple of years and then return home. But the native people are there permanently.
The other thing I would like to mention in the debate is the nature of cost in the North as compared to the South. It may be that southern Canadians should be subsidizing northern Canadians for two reasons; first, we are all part of the North. We feel like northerners even though 90 per cent of us live along or near the borders of the United States. But we all have this kind of northern feeling that this is Canada and we are a northern country. We are quite proud of the pioneers in the North and we have a great deal of respect for the survival of our native people both Indian and Inuit in the North. So I feel we should be thinking about the cost of living in the north, not just in housing but in energy as well.
People in the North pay 80 cents a litre for gasoline. People in Toronto pay 40 cents a litre. Compare the price of gasoline and housing in Rosedale with the price of gasoline and housing in Yellowknife. It may be that if people in the South pay one tenth of a cent a litre more for gasoline there will be a sort of postage stamp price for gasoline in the North so that people pay the same price. A postage stamp costs the same in Yellowknife as it does in Rosedale or in Vancouver-Kingsway. Perhaps gasoline should be treated like that, and perhaps housing should as well.
We want to see our North developed in good ways. We can look at how the Soviets have developed their North. I am not suggesting we follow along in their way. I do not like the way they deal with culture and so on. However, if we compare the number of people the Soviets have living in their North to the number of people we have living in our North-a much lesser amount-the Soviet way could be instructive. This, of course, fits in as well with the Government's wish, which we support, to proclaim in the loudest possible terms Canadian sovereignty in that area.
We support the Bill, Mr. Speaker. We understand the technical principles of what has to be condominium development. There are other housing problems in the North which the Minister should look at, and perhaps we should look at, and that is, the broad picture of some sort of northern subsidies so that people can live in the North at a cost equal to the cost of living in the South. I said that my remarks would be brief, so I had better sit down.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Mr. McLean, for Miss MacDonald, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands, seconded by Mr. Crombie, moves that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, be now read a second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to indicate my pleasure at speaking to this Bill and the important matters relating to immigration for which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has asked me to assume responsibility along with my colleague.
As Hon. Members of the House will be aware, Bill C-55 proposes several amendments to our present Immigration Act. These amendments, Mr. Speaker, are minor in nature. They are designed to increase the flexibility and capacity of the Immigration Appeal Board to deal with a greater number of cases.
Under the current Act, the maximum number of board members is restricted to 18. Bill C-55 would increase this number to a maximum of 50. The Immigration Appeal Board reviews appeals of family class applications which have been refused abroad. It hears appeals against deportation orders by certain people who have come to Canada and have not been admitted or who, having been admitted, have run afoul of the Immigration Act. The Board also makes a redetermination of refugee claims which have been evaluated by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee but subsequently rejected by the Minister. All of these categories of cases are important, but the Board has far more work at present than it can do. Hence, the urgency to pass this legislation.
Bill C-55 will permit the appointment over time of new members to cope with the workload. In addition, the number of vice-chairs will be increased from five to 13, giving the Board even greater flexibility. The Bill would also require that not fewer than half of the vice-chairs be members of a provincial bar for at least five years.
To ensure that board members are used effectively, the Bill would permit the chairman to delegate responsibility on technical matters to one-member panels. In previous committee discussion there were some concerns expressed regarding the matter of one-member panels. I have had an opportunity to talk with the spokespersons for the opposition Parties and we are agreed that it would be in the interest of all that a three-person panel be maintained. We will encourage the adoption of an amendment in committee in this regard.
Immigration Act, 1976
There are two distinct reasons for the Immigration Appeal Board requesting expansion over the last two years. The first is the increasing volume of appeal cases in such matters as family class applications, deportation orders and other rulings by the independent immigration adjudicators. At present the Board has a backlog of some 1,400 of those cases. The load is growing at the rate of over 140 per month. These appeals usually require at least half a day for disposition, and some can take as long as two weeks or more. In addition to that burden, the IAB is also responsible for hearings regarding redetermination of refugee status. The Board has faced an increasing number of cases concerning refugees in the past few years. The rate of increase exceeded the Board's ability to respond and this has created a backlog in refugee matters as well. This backlog increased dramatically as a result of the Supreme Court of Canada's ruling in the Singh case. Prior to that, the IAB dealt only with refugee redetermination. That is, the Board heard appeals from the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. The Singh case has changed the procedure and requires that the Board hold an oral hearing for every person who wishes a redetermination of his or her claim to refugee status. Thus the IAB now faces a backlog of some 14,000 refugee cases. This extraordinary backlog has also limited the Board's ability to deal with the backlog of other appeals. Clearly it is important that we respond to the Supreme Court of Canada decision and do it quickly and not appear in any way to be questioning the validity of that decision. This is the aim of the Government in introducing this legislation.
Before returning to the workload of the Board, I should mention briefly the work of Rabbi Gunther Plaut. As Members of the House will know, for the past year Rabbi Plaut has been studying the Board and the delicate question of refugee determination. His report, which was tabled in the House by my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), last June, treats this problem in a sensitive and thorough manner. Later this fall legislation will be introduced stemming from both a review of Rabbi Plaut's report and the views of interested Canadians. This legislation will form the basis of a new refugee determination system, a new commitment to those in need. What I should like to make clear at this point to all Members of the House and the public is that the legislation we are discussing today is in no way connected to this larger legislative reform which will be proposed later in the year. What we seek to do now is to equip the IAB to deal with its immediate and pressing needs. Hence, the proposal to increase the membership of the Board to a maximum of 50 members. Because there have been some concerns expressed that this adjustment might in some way affect the commitment regarding the refugee redetermination review and proposed legislation, I have agreed, in discussion with concerned members and the opposition critics, that it may be important to accept an amendment regarding the length of time new members will serve in order to indicate clearly that this is an emergency reaction to a specific situation.

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
In addition to the refugee claims' backlog there are also more than 1,000 family sponsorship appeals pending. Families which cannot be reunited because of a legal prohibition must now wait for more than a year to determine whether relief may be possible. I do not need to remind Members of this House that family reunification is a corner-stone of the Immigration Act and Canadians are confused as to why, if this is so, we cannot act on family reunification. I know, from my contact with Members of Parliament that their constituency offices are inundated with questions about the time taken up by these procedures. Therefore, it will be important that we move quickly to have these amendments made in committee and have the Bill completed.
Some of these cases, of course, involve the parents of Canadians for whom long delays cannot be sustained. Bill C-55 goes further than simply reducing the delay for these people. It extends the right of appeal to permanent residents, that is, those whom we refer to as landed immigrants, as well as to Canadian citizens. At present, the right of appeal is available only to sponsors who are Canadian citizens. It is the Government's view that this is not consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and therefore we wish to act and act quickly on this matter. Hence, Bill C-55 will grant the right of appeal to landed immigrants who are permanent residents as well as to Canadian citizens.
The amendments to the Immigration Act contained in this Bill are the result of careful consideration and our desire to meet the requirements not only of Canadians but also of the Supreme Court ruling. I believe these amendments will address the serious backlog and other operational issues now hampering the process. I am happy to seek an accommodation of concerns, as I have already mentioned, regarding the size of the panels, and to answer that concern. I am also prepared to recognize the importance of a stated time period for appointments which will indicate that this is an emergency measure and not a long-term permanent arrangement that would in any way threaten the present discussions about refugee determination.
This House knows that Canada has long extended a hand to those suffering repression or displacement. We have offered countless thousands of people an opportunity to start new lives here. We have also shown compassion and sensitivity regarding the desire of families to be reunited. This Bill will retain our humanitarian traditions in these areas and I ask all Members of the House to give it their support so that we can move speedily on this issue in order to begin to alleviate the present backlog and with it the human hardship and agony that is involved.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and Hon. Members for your attention to this important matter.

I thank you and the Members of the House.
First, the Minister has announced some changes to the original Bill. Would he confirm that the change is that the Immigration Appeal Board remains at a quorum of three members to hear sponsorship appeals?
Second, did the Minister mention in his speech any reduction in the number of board members? The Bill proposes to increase the board members from 18 to 50. Is he staying with the number of 50 or going to a smaller number? Those are my questions.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question of clarification. On the first point, I have heard representations with regard to the three-person panels and I am prepared to accept that. However, three-person panels require more person-power. It would defeat the purpose to insist upon a lower number. You cannot have it both ways. If you are going to have increased panels, then you need the capacity. The Bill specifies a maximum of up to 50 members and, in concert with the chairman of the IAB, these members have to be found, trained, and phased in. There is some flexibility to allow for greater sensitivity in carrying out this work, but I will be open to a definition of the term of office of these new appointees which will indicate that they are not intended to provide long-term solutions.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to speak to Bill C-55, introduced in the House today by the Minister of State for Immigration.
September 26, 1985

Although we have had several meetings with the Minister, I have a few comments and observations regarding this Bill, whose purpose is to amend the Immigration Act.
I hope, in my comments, to clarify the motives of the Liberal Party for objecting to its passage. Bill C-55 would increase the maximum number of members of the Immigration Appeal Board to 50 and the maximum number of vicechairmen to thirteen, and would permit the Immigration Appeal Board to hold hearings.
On April 4 of this year, in its ruling in the Singh case, as the Minister mentioned earlier, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that the Immigration Appeal Board had to hold oral hearings of claimants seeking refugee status. The present procedure does not provide for oral hearings. At the first level, the Advisory Committee on the Status of Refugees, a decision whether or not to grant refugee status is made on the basis of the transcript of an interview conducted by an immigration officer upon the claimant's arrival in this country.
At the second level, that is, the Immigration Appeal Board, the same transcript serves as the documentary basis for the appeal decision.
I would now like to speak more specifically to Bill C-55. One of the reasons I am opposed to the Bill is that legislation that is supposed to be a provisional measure will probably become the cornerstone of the future process for determining refugee status. The Minister is giving us the assurance that it is a temporary measure, but we all know that when the Government says temporary, a measure may be temporary for as long as five or ten years.
As the House is aware, a new Bill to reform the entire procedure is to be tabled shortly. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has started a series of consultations on the subject which are to be concluded shortly, as soon as the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration has heard a series of witnesses. In fact, I know the Minister will be in Montreal next Saturday. We can therefore expect a new Bill very shortly, and I think adopting Bill C-55 at this stage would be prejudicial to future reform. One of my reasons for making this assumption, Mr. Speaker, is based on the selection and mandate of Immigration Appeal Board members.
At a hearing held by the Standing Committee in February of this year, it became clear that to attract competent and committed members to the Immigration Appeal Board, it was advisable to provide for terms of as long as five and even ten years. The reasoning behind this position was that a person could not be asked to give up a career temporarily to work on the Board. The Minister told us today that they are perhaps willing in committee . . . the Government would therefore be willing to change and we would have terms varying from three to five years instead of ten years. Last February, no one challenged this reasoning and I believe the Members of all three parties were in agreement.
Immigration Act, 1976
But to get back to Bill C-55, I would like to point out to my colleagues opposite that the Bill is proposing the exact opposite. It is suggesting an increase in the number of members, which would be a temporary way of dealing with the painful problem of case backlogs at the Immigration Appeal Board.
However, quite frankly, how can we expect to attract competent people if they are told their services will no longer be required in another six months or a year, that is, when the new determination process will be implemented?
Mr. Speaker, despite the reform, I believe the Minister of Employment and Immigration has already decided on the structure and membership of the Immigration Appeal Board, and has done so while ignoring the suggestions made in the Plaut Report and the many critical comments regarding the Board made by the Supreme Court.
The Plaut Report does not really allow much room for the Immigration Appeal Board. To be more specific, I would say there is no mention of the Board in any of the three models proposed by Rabbi Plaut. Appeals are included in the models, but their exact form is not clearly defined.
I think it is rather significant that the Appeal Board was not even considered as a possible alternate solution in the Plaut Report. Incidentally, I might point out that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration released the report exactly ten weeks after she received it, and seven weeks after she announced that it would be made public in a matter of days.
The Board's adversary system has been challenged by many lawyers and organizations which look after refugees. A colleague reminded the parliamentary committee of some cases where the Board insisted that an applicant for refugee status prove that he would be subject to persecution. Well, that is not what the Act provides, it does not require applicants to prove that they would be subject to persecution in their country of origin, but only that they are afraid of being persecuted, and that is altogether different.
Some people believe that the backlog of cases would melt away if Bill C-55 were to be adopted. Unfortunately this suggestion does not take into account the fact that cases now before the High Court-the Federal Court-will go back to appeal where the backlog will swell beyond limits. The main objective of Bill C-55 is therefore unattainable the way things are now. This fact was emphasized during a standing committee hearing last June and I am surprised that the Conservative Government still wants to steer this course to nowhere.
The whole exercise is off on a tangent and badly documented because the initial proceedings do not include a hearing with refugee status applicants, and it is sheer aberration to believe that increasing the number of commissioners will guarantee better equity. When the first stage of a proceeding is marred by injustices, the situation will not be redressed at the second stage of the proceeding, no matter how extraordinary it may be.
7042

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
Bill C-55 is an attempt to restore some form of equity in a process which we all know cannot possibly accomplish what it is supposed to do in the first place. Consequently, Bill C-55 is useless.
I would also like to point out that during a parliamentary committee hearing in June we learned that, besides reducing the backlog of refugee cases, increasing the number of Immigration Appeal Board members would also expedite the settlement of cases of sponsored immigrants and of deported immigrants.
There is nothing untoward in that, Mr. Speaker, but then nobody should pretend that refugee status applicants will be denied justice if we prevent the passage of Bill C-55.
That was the main argument of the Conservative Government in June when it attempted to get a consensus from all three parties to adopt the Bill. In that respect, allow me to quote the remarks of a lawyer who appeared before the standing committee in June:
As a lawyer I have the clear impression that, from September to December when hundreds of cases will be brought back to the Appeal Board, those people will have to be represented by counsel. The lawyers will have to work with files full of shortcomings with respect to the presentation of the cases themselves. I therefore have the impression that a new backlog will be created at the Appeal Board. There are so many outstanding cases at this stage that we have a feeling in Montreal that the middle-term temporary solution being considered by the Appeal Board could not sufficiently reduce the backlog of refugee cases that justice would be done and that we could look to a reform in due time.
The Liberal Party is opposed to Bill C-55 because it contains the basis for part of a new process to grant refugee status and because this does not take into account the Plaut Report and all the requests which have been made by the organizations dealing with refugees.
If the Progressive Conservative Government is serious and honest when it consults these organizations before any reform of the process for granting refugee status, it should not try to pass a bill which contains the basis for the future process.
This view is largely shared by immigration lawyers and many humanitarian organizations. They include the Table de concertation aupres des refugies, SOS-Refugies, the Civil Liberties Union, the Societe quebecoise de la solidarity international, the Immigration Lawyers Association, the Association des Juristes quebecois, the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees, the Standing Conference of Canadian Organizations concerned for refugees, Amnesty International and the Inland Refugee Society of British Columbia.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party is not opposing Bill C-55 simply for the sake of it. This is not a partisan issue, but a question of common sense.
It is time to reform the process for granting refugee status and to undertake a comprehensive information compaign on refugees. The very great majority of Canadian men and
women do not differentiate between a refugee and an immigrant.
In the case of the immigrant, the host country has the right to set criteria and to accept only those who meet them. It is quite different for the refugee. Indeed, Canada has international obligations. According to the Geneva Convention, the applicant for refugee status is entitled to get help; this is not a privilege, but a right.
Most of our fellow citizens and many Members of Parliament are not aware of this. Many forget about the difficult political situations which exist throughout the world. When we are familiar with the international situation of apartheid in South Africa, of the military dictatorships and police repressions in many Latin American countries, of the religious intolerance in Iran, of the invasion of Afghanistan and so on, we are more willing to welcome those who are afraid of persecutions in their own country and who seek refuge in Canada.
As Rabbi Plaut emphasizes, compared with the scope of the worldwide refugee problem, the task of recognizing the status of people who apply for refugee status here in Canada is relatively small.
In addition to establishing the difference between immigrants and refugees, the information campaign that we need should emphasize the economic contribution of the new-comers. We have to eliminate the myth that foreigners steal jobs from Canadian men and women.
Many economic studies on immigrants show that it is impossible to establish a cause and effect relationship between the number of foreigners admitted to the country and the economic situation. However, some economists state that by increasing the number of potential consumers in a market, the immigrants make a positive contribution to the economy.
In other words, it is our entire approach to immigration which must be improved as we must become more open-minded while maintaining the generous attitude which has long been the characteristic of Canadian men and women.
This urgently needed change in attitudes should go hand in hand with the reform of the process for granting refugee status. It seems to me that the implementation of this new process gives us an ideal opportunity to initiate a nationwide debate on the refugee issue.
The band-aid solution now proposed by the Conservative Government in Bill C-55 therefore seems to me both useless and harmful. If the bill is passed, I believe that it would unfortunately take a lot of time for the Government to reform the whole process for granting refugee status, contrary to the wishes of a great many organizations working with refugees.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am somewhat concerned that the Government, on such an
September 26, 1985

important matter as immigration, did not give immigration critics, in particular the critic for our Party, very much notice of its intention. Unfortunately our critic was unable to be present because of that fact. I feel it is a disservice to immigrants to be dealing with Bills in this ad hoc manner.
However, because I represent the riding of Vancouver East, which has a very high proportion of immigrants, both landed immigrants and their families and refugees from many countries of the world, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on their behalf. There are a number of reasons for our being concerned about the Bill. We are very concerned, as is the Government, about the backlog of cases. Many immigrants who have been trying to get their families into Canada have been waiting, in some cases, for years. It has been very difficult for them when they are refused a proper hearing. The change in procedure to allow oral hearings-and certainly it is a change in the right direction-has increased this backlog. I understand that there is something like 20,000 cases in total in the backlog; perhaps it is even more than that at this time. Some 13,800 of these cases are refugee cases. I can imagine the concern of these people who are desperate to remain in Canada or to have their relatives come to this country.
We agree completely that the situation is very critical, but our real concern is about the ad hockery of this legislation which deals with only a small aspect of the problem.

subsubtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF FUNDS TO CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government's announcement that it would allocate all funds for defending victims of discrimination to a single agency was a mistake. I believe that funds earmarked for defending women should have been allocated to the Women's Legal Education and Action Fund, and I deplore the fact that
the Government put all its eggs in one basket by directing all funds for defending victims of discrimination to a single agency.
Mr. Speaker, I have absolutely nothing against the Canadian Council of Social Development, but it is not the ideal vehicle for women to organize and take significant action to defend their rights.

If the Government had given the Legal Education and Action Fund the money to defend women, it would have permitted them to set their own priorities. Now with the Canadian Council on Social Development, the money will be given on a case by case basis. The same work will be done twice and we will lose time and money.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POLAR INSTITUTE-LACK OF INUIT REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (Mr. Crombie) appointed a three member committee to make recommendations for the establishment of a National Polar Institute for Canada. Unfortunately the Inuit are not represented on this committee. Inuit people will not be involved in making basic recommendations for an institute dealing with their home territory.
It is important for southern Canadians to remember that when it comes to dealing with the Arctic, Inuit people have expertise which cannot be duplicated by academic degrees or scientific and organizational know-how.
In any future development in the Arctic, the Inuit are the people most directly affected. Surely the Minister must know that the time has passed when southern based academics and bureaucrats can make basis decisions affecting Inuit people without their involvement. Time for their involvement is at the beginning of the process, not halfway down the line. I urge the Minister to remember his responsibilities and to add at least one Inuit to the committee.

subsubtopic: DANGER CREATED BY FRENCH NUCLEAR TESTS IN THE PACIFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read in the press that the French Prime Minister was to attend

September 26, 1985
underground nuclear tests of neutron bombs to be conducted on an atoll in the Pacific Ocean.
As a Member of Parliament and as a Canadian, I find it intolerable that any country on this planet should continue to conduct nuclear tests without knowing the possible impact on the earth's crust and without advising other countries.
I therefore urge the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in my Government to enquire about the exact date of the last nuclear tests conducted in the Pacific by the French. There is no doubt in my mind that all Canadians and the various peace movements in Canada are opposed to the conducting of any tests of this kind.

subsubtopic: GRAIN ELEVATOR IN BIG RIVER, SASK.-LOCAL FARMERS' SUCCESS STORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons should be aware of the efforts of some innovative farmers in north central Saskatchewan.
One year ago the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool announced it would be closing the grain elevator in Big River. Farmers in the surrounding area, after protesting the closure in vain, formed a co-operative to explore some possibilities on their own. As their member of Parliament, I worked closely with these farmers and met with them on several occasions.
The farmers were also successfully helped by their MLA, the Hon. Colin Maxwell, and on one occasion we met with Canadian Transport Commissioner Jim McDonough, who provided technical advice. The farmers were able to purchase the Big River elevator from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, sign a lease with CN Rail and enlist the assistance of Pioneer Grain to help them manage the elevator. Special thanks should be directed to a former Member of this House, the Hon. Otto Lang, now of Pioneer Grain. Mr. Lang was instrumental in aiding the farmers' cause.
I would like to pay tribute to all the farmers who made this venture possible, particularly Big River farmer Eugene Swanson. At a time when there are many problems in Canadian agriculture, it is reassuring to hear a farming success story.

Mr. Speaker, while it was very good news to learn on September 25, 1985, from the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) that the federaL Government has finally committed itself to providing funds to assist with legal expenses for those seeking their rights
to equality in accordance with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, my colleagues and I are greatly concerned about the way in which the Government proposes to administer and allocate these funds.
These funds are needed to pay for the cost of challenges in court. They are needed by many groups which have been disadvantaged until now by unequal treatment, namely, the women of Canada, the native people, the handicapped, and members of various multicultural groups. These groups constitute a huge majority of the people of Canada who, until now, have been denied equal rights.
Why does the Government seem to insist on giving all these important funds on a case by case basis through the Canadian Council on Social Development? In asking this, 1 want to affirm my respect for the outstanding work of the Canadian Council on Social Development, which has been entrusted with responsibility for assigning financial support for court challenges.
It is how these funds are assigned that is of critical importance. The principle of the Government being at arms length is also important. But why does the Government not guarantee, as these constituent groups have demanded, that adequate funds be given to the organizations responsible for an over-all approach? They are the groups affected, and they are the ones who are qualified to decide the priorities, timing, and issues that are appropriate. Women understand the issues of women. Canadian natives understand those that concern natives, and the handicapped know what their approach must be. Each of these major groups has its views-

Mr. Speaker, the year 1985 marks the one-hundredth anniversary of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is unfortunate that this anniversary also marks the rescinding of an historic right for railway employees, namely, the suspension of all CP Railway travel passes for retired employees.
Railway employees have had travel privileges on Canadian railways since 1856. Canadian National continues to honour this right of retirees.
The CPR has given no reason for this mean treatment of those who have given the railway so many years of faithful service. The only explanation offered has been that it is a matter of "principle". It is apparently a CPR principle to cut off this small concession to retired workers at the same time it is celebrating 100 years of successful operation made possible by the work of its employees.
September 26, 1985

It is apparently a CPR principle to stop any rail travel by over 65s at the same time that it is paying salaries to senior executives well in excess of $500,000 annually.
This display of unparallelled meanness and lack of understanding leads me to bestow on the CPR the title of "Corporate Scrooge of the Year" for its failure to keep faith with its former employees.
As part of this award, I wish that all CP executives and board members be forced to watch repeated showings of their own television advertisements which proclaim that an employee "is never just a number with CP". This, of course, is true. The CPR continues to show by its actions-

Mr. Speaker, it is with great honour that I bring to the attention of this House the celebrations today throughout the world of World Maritime Day.
On behalf of Canada, I would like to offer congratulations on this occasion to the International Maritime Organization based in London, England, and to its esteemed Secretary General, Mr. C.P. Srivastava for a very successful year.
During its 26 years of existence, IMO has been instrumental in improving maritime safety. Canada was a founding member and has played a significant role in the development of IMO. At present, Mr. W. A. O'Neil, president of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, is Chairman of IMO Council.
The theme of World Maritime Day for 1985 is Maritime Search and Rescue. The survival of persons in distress at sea depends ultimately on the speed with which they are located and rescued. The most important provisions on global search and rescue are embodied in the International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue adopted by IMO in 1979. The Convention adopts improvements to existing procedures and introduces new requirements in order to facilitate speedy and effective action at both national and international levels.
It is with great honour and personal pleasure that I commend the convention and its objectives to the Canadian maritime community on this occasion. May I, on behalf of this House, convey to the International Maritime Organization, to seafarers in Canada and throughout the world, our greetings and good wishes on their continuing efforts-

subtopic: CALL FOR CANADIAN OWNERSHIP OF FACTORY FREEZER TRAWLERS
CALL FOR CANADIAN OWNERSHIP OF FACTORY FREEZER TRAWLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time the Canadian Government does not permit the ownership of factory freezer trawlers by Canadian companies. The international market, however, recognizes that supply of fresh product is assured from freezer trawlers, as the appropriate technology has proven.
The nations that operate FFTs are benefiting from this market preference at the expense of Canadian companies. The ability of National Sea Products to remain competitive in the world market is therefore limited unless it is granted the requested licence to avail itself of FFT technology.
There are some people in Atlantic Canada who are saying that one freezer trawler will affect the supplies of northern cod. This statement is not in line with the facts since we presently have operating within our 200-mile-zone a total of 74 factory freezer trawlers: eight from Cuba; eight from West Germany; nine from France; one from East Germany; seven from Japan; one from Poland; eight from Portugal, and 32 from the U.S.S.R.
I believe that the time has arrived when we must reassess our priorities as they relate to quotas for foreign and Canadian fishermen within our 200-mile zone. FFTs will enable Canadians to find new job opportunities and open up markets now lost to foreign competition. Seventy-four factory ships for foreigners in Canadian waters and none for Canadians is no longer acceptable. It is time that we got on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is on a disastrous course:
This Government has embarked upon a course which could propel Canadian scientific inquiry backward and leave the country far behind other countries in scientific achievement.
These are the words of Nobel prize winner Gerhard Herz-berg. And what is the Government doing about this situation which threatens Canada's future?
At a meeting with his provincial counterparts recently the Minister for Science and Technology said: "Canada faces strong international economic challenges". But this sober assessment is betrayed by his cowardly conclusion: "We have recognized the vital importance of science and technology to meeting these challenges".
This is not good enough. Canadians will not accept that the Government completely ignore their future. Time after time, blunder after blunder, the Government has shown that it cannot recognize a problem until it is too late. Mr. Speaker, this stinks.

September 26, 1985
It is time that the Government do something about Canada's future and chart a course for Canada's science community. Unless more resources are allocated to this important sector, it will take a miracle for this country ever again to have a Nobel prize winner.

Mr. Speaker, according to Canada Post official statements published recently in the newspapers, not only must the corporation reduce its deficit, but it has to show a profit as well.
Though I agree with that statement, I want to warn the corporation that it should not be done at the expense of the Canadian people for it might unnecessarily create a new category of second class citizens.
Unfortunate though it may be, Mr. Speaker, I have to say that an ever growing number of my constituents keep complaining and asking for improved postal services.
We all agree on the need for new rationalization standards, but we have to keep in mind that the ridings are not all the same, that most of them are located in rural or semi-urban areas. Perhaps it would be better to make those standards reflect the reality of such ridings so that highly urbanized ridings will not get better services at the expense of other ridings.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully urge the Minister responsible for Canada Post to pay particular attention to the situation and keep a close watch on the development of the Crown corporation with a view to making appropriate changes and restoring a fair balance.

Mr. Speaker, the concern expressed yesterday by my Leader about the possibility of Canadian uranium being used for nuclear weapons should cause all of us to pay more attention not just to that but to nuclear issues in general. I would like to bring three of them to the attention of the Government.
There is a conference in London this week having to do with the disposal of pollutants at sea and I would like to encourage the Government not to support the American position that the two-year moratorium on the disposal of radioactive wastes in
the ocean should be discontinued. I would encourage the Government to support the extension of the moratorium.
I would also encourage the Government to take a serious look at whether or not the sale of tritium could be included in the agreements which now exist with respect to prohibiting the use of Canadian uranium for the development of nuclear weapons.
Finally, I would like to encourage the Government to remember the promise of the Conservatives in 1979 that they would set up an inquiry into the whole nuclear fuel cycle in this country, from uranium mining to radioactive waste disposal, and cause that inquiry to begin so that Canadians can have a say, for a change, in the nuclear future that was imposed on them by the Liberals and seems to be business as usual by the Conservatives. We would like to see an opportunity for Canadians to have a say.
