subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform the House and the country that I have today spoken to the President of the United States to express Canada's interests in pursuing a new trade agreement between our two countries.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
We hope that this action will lead to negotiations for a new trade agreement between the United States and Canada. I have asked the President to explore with Congress their interest in pursuing these negotiations. Both sides recognize that the issues are complex. Both sides are determined to see the process moved as expeditiously as possible. The President and I will be meeting in the spring of 1986 to review progress and the prospects for a new agreement.

Hon. Members will recall that at Quebec City six months ago, President Reagan and I made a declaration on trade in goods and services. We pledged to explore all possible ways to reduce and eliminate existing barriers in our bilateral trade. We instructed the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and the President's Trade Representative to report on how trade could be enhanced between our two countries. Today I will table the Minister's report to me on this vitally important subject. Of course, we will make it public, Mr. Speaker.

Throughout our history trade has been critical to Canada's livelihood. Now, almost one-third of what we produce is exported. Few countries in the world are so dependent upon trade. Trade simply means jobs. Yet, our share of world trade has been declining. This trend ultimately threatens the jobs of many Canadians and the living standards of the nation as a whole. We must confront this threat. We must, as a nation, reverse this trend. To do so we need a better, a fairer, and more predictable trade relationship with the United States. At stake are more than two million jobs which depend directly on Canadian access to the U.S. market.
Five decades ago the world was in the midst of the great depression. Restrictive trade policies made things worse. Canada and the U.S. were the first to respond to the strong protectionist pressures of the time. They began the process of tearing down these obstacles to growth. Canada and the United States indeed concluded a bilateral trade agreement in 1935. More countries joined them in 1938. The principles underlying the Canadian-American bilateral agreement formed the foundation of the post-war multilateral trading system.



September 26, 1985
Statements by Ministers
For half a century Canada has pursued consistently a policy of trade liberalization. Today, more than ever, our prosperity and that of our partners depend on an expanding world trade and a growing world economy. In all the forums where Canada is present, we are working to remove the impediments to trade, aid, investment and development on a global basis.
[ Translation]
In particular we are playing a leading role in promoting and preparing for a new round of multilateral trade negotiations in the GATT. We are consulting the less developed countries on issues of common concern; and we emphatically support their participation in the negotiations.
No responsible person anywhere today advocates protectionism as a national economic strategy. Yet, sector by sector, region by region, country by country, Canada included, there persists the impulse to protectionism, whenever the going gets tough. Protectionist measures are always advocated as exceptional cases. But the barriers grow more numerous, more ingenious and more insidious all the time. Sometimes these measures are aimed directly at Canadian products or services; often they are aimed at others, but catch us in the process. The motive may be laudable. The effect may be incremental. But in any overall reckoning, protectionist mesures are always self-defeating. This impulse to protectionism is defensive and negative-yet entirely understandable in human terms. This is what we are up against, Mr. Speaker.

Economics, geography, common sense and the national interest dictate that we try to secure and expand our trade with our closest and largest trading partner. To do so is fully consistent with our commitment to freer trade on a multilateral basis. Of course, any new agreement between Canada and the United States would have to meet the test of our overriding obligations under the GATT.
Five decades ago, national Governments turned inward to shield their peoples from economic distress. Ultimately, protectionism proved suicidal. It brought on the great depression with all its attendant misery.
The Government will be pursuing clear goals in our talks with the United States. We are two sovereign democracies in every way, sharing the same continent. It seems to me that reaching out with our maturity and strengths to seek out ways of enhancing mutual beneficial trade goals is an honourable course of action.
The need to secure our access to the U.S. market was the dominant theme of representations made in all parts of the country to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) during his extensive consultations last spring and summer. The same message was heard by the Senate-House of Commons committee which reported in late August. Hon. Members will have taken note of the conclusions of the Macdonald Commission, together with its impressive analysis and documentation. Canadians will also be aware of the strong representations on
trade which have been made by their provincial Premiers over the last several months. I have taken care, and shall continue to take special care, as I did this afternoon by speaking personally with all provincial Premiers in advance, to consult with my fellow First Ministers on an ongoing basis as the process unfolds. To that end, I have placed this major issue on the agenda at the meeting of First Ministers in November. The Government will also arrange, if possible, a full debate in the House on the subject at a time agreeable to Hon. Members.
We must all be aware that international negotiations are complex and extremely challenging. Success is not a sure thing, but the results of success are well worth the enormous effort and good faith required for these negotiations. Moreover, we have already agreed to establish a special mechanism with the provinces, to ensure their continuing involvement throughout the process. To support Canada's negotiating effort, the Minister of International Trade is creating a new consultative arrangement with business, labour and other groups.
I emphasize that we are beginning a process of purely commercial negotiations with the United States of America, the results of which would provide sufficient time for all Canadians to plan ahead to take advantage of new opportunities which come with enhanced access. We seek to negotiate the broadest possible package of mutually beneficial reductions in tariff and non-tariff barriers between our two countries. I accept the words of prudence coming to us from some quarters, indeed from some quarters of the House, on this subject. I accept those words and I respect them. We understand the natural concerns of various sectors and regions that their interests as well be recognized both in the negotiations and in any agreement. Of course, this shall be the case.
However, there is general consensus that we must seek to secure and improve our trade with the United States. To shrink from this challenge and opportunity would be an act of timidity unworthy of Canada. It would be contrary to our national interest. Our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to fight regional disparities, our unique cultural identity, our special linguistic character- these are the essence of Canada. They are not at issue in these negotiations.

I have not had the opportunity of reading or inspecting the report of the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) to the Prime Minister and of course can make no comment on it. There is no blueprint in that speech. He does not set the parameters as to where he would like the negotiations to go. Frankly I say to him, not having read the fundamental document which he tabled, that the speech itself was not worthy of the importance of the subject to Canadians.

speechtext:
The issue of free trade is the most critical issue facing the Canadian economy. Our relationship with the United States has implications for all regions and all economic sectors of Canada. Negotiations will be vital for every business, for every working man and woman in the country.

Mr. Speaker, the question has been considered very closely. I know it was dealt with in a C.D. Howe Research Institute report and, quite recently, the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on Canada's International Relations has made a full examination of the issue. I take this opportunity to congratulate my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) and the Hon. for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), on their outstanding contribution to the proceedings and especially to the conclusions of the committee.
Mr. Speaker, the position of our Party is quite simply summed up in one of the committee's conclusions. I quote from page 38 of the parliamentary report:
The Committee recommends that there be immediate bilateral trade discussions with the United States.
The discussions should centre initially on resolving current trade irritants, especially the prevention of the imposition of additional non-tariff barriers to trade between the two countries. Issues such as the definition of the net effect of subsidies provided by both sides and the identification of the appropriate jurisdictional authority for implementing changes in non-tariff barriers should be
Statements by Ministers
dealt with explicitly. These discussions should be used to explore the potential for additional trade liberalization between the two countries and for securing and strengthening access to each other's markets. Issues such as trade in services, government procurement, and reducing remaining tariff barriers should be dealt with explicitly.
Now, the following passage is very important:
The Committee views these discussions as the natural extension of a process begun by Prime Minister Mulroney and President Reagan at Quebec City. The Committee believes that it is premature for Canada to initiate formal bilateral negotiations but that it is necessary to initiate broad discussions with the United States to determine their receptivity to liberalizing bilateral trade. After a ministerial report to Parliament on the outcome of these discussions and on whether certain conditions have been met, the government should decide whether the prospects are sufficiently promising to continue on to detailed negotiations.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our position.
The Government, on the other hand, has moved a stage further than that and, we believe, prematurely. I cite what the Prime Minister said this afternoon. He said, "We hope that this action will lead to negotiations for a new trade agreement between the United States and Canada". He is asking the President to advise the Congress, which is the initial step into the initiation of such negotiations. This goes beyond what the parliamentary committee recommended and for good reasons.
We are concerned that before entering formal negotiations with the United States we, in Parliament, and the country as a whole should know the full parameters of the Canadian position. We want to know what the exemptions will be, what adjustments will be required and what assistance will be given to our working force. We will want to know how the country and how the United States will respond to non-tariff barriers. We would like a blueprint of the general tactic and the general scheme of the negotiations. We have not had that.
We consider that the Government is launching upon this exercise with the United States with inadequate prior discussion in Parliament and without revealing its negotiating position or the parameters of that position in any detail. Obviously there has to be give and take in the negotiations, but we would have preferred a more specific proposition presented to this Parliament.
I can understand and echo what the Prime Minister said; that this is a very crucial negotiation for this country. We have a huge market in the United States. It has 220 million people as against the Canadian population of 25 million. Seventy per cent of our exports go to the United States, representing some $80 billion in 1984.
What we are saying, Sir, is that we must have an honest and open debate on the parameters and on the cost of benefits of any arrangements with the United States. We must know what it is that the Government is trying to accomplish. We cannot go into this discussion without having a better idea of where the Government stands.
I noticed that the Prime Minister mentioned a parliamentary debate. I have it in his text, and he has repeated it here

this afternoon. On page 4 of his text we find that the Government would also arrange, if possible, a debate in this House on the subject of trade at a time agreeable to Hon. Members. Not "if possible", there must be a debate on this issue and it must be early and it must be full. We want a far better knowledge of the position which the Government intends to take and the full scope of the negotiations.
The Macdonald Commission, headed by Donald Macdonald, a former colleague of ours, of mine, and a good friend, suggested that we take what was termed "a leap of faith on free trade". But this is too big a jump. We must go into these negotiations with our eyes open. The Government is not telling us the whole story. In fact, we are not even sure which Minister is in charge.
Initially, at the time of the Quebec Summit, the Prime Minister reserved in his own office and to his own purview the subject of bilateral negotiations and bilateral relations with the United States. speechtext:
I want to thank Members from all sides of the House, Mr. Speaker. This is a fundamental issue affecting this country and we want to state our position as clearly as we can at this stage on the basis of the documentation we have.
The President speaks of free trade. He includes in that speech mention of strike forces and war chests to ensure that U.S. industry and business are protected and defended from outside competition. In other words, he is protecting himself and keeping his elbows very close to his ribs. The speech has a schizophrenic view, a protectionist underpinning to a vocabulary and to a rhetoric of free trade.
There are also increasing numbers of countervailing requests filed with the United States International Trade Commission and the U.S. Department of Commerce. This country is facing not only legislative barriers but we are also facing judicial barriers that the litigious process of the United States allows so freely.
I ask the Government, and I hope we will get an answer when we get an opportunity to debate this: how does the Government propose to deal with the conflicting approaches of the legislative and executive branches of the U.S. Government and the seeming inconsistency in the President's own statement?
Another important question in our mind: does the President of the United States have the power to deliver? It is quite clear that if the Prime Minister finally finds a direction, pursues it with some vigour, pursues it with some determination, he has the majority in the House of Commons to carry it. The President has no such power. The Prime Minister knows full well that there is a separation of powers under the U.S. constitution. With every month that passes, the President of the United States has less influence with that Congress, whether it be on tax reform, on the budgetary deficit and, I venture to say and suggest to the Prime Minister, on the question of free trade as well. With every month that passes he becomes more of a lame duck. The Prime Minister and his Government have already lost a valuable first year of their mandate and a valuable first year of the President's own
September 26, 1985

mandate in failing to bring this matter before the House and before the discussion process.

I think the Prime Minister is right to admit that the position of provincial governments will have a vital impact on the discussions or negotiations. How will purchasing policies, established in this country by the provinces, affect negotiations? How does the Government intend to respond to the needs of the provinces in trade negotiations?
What is the Prime Minister going to say to his provincial First Minister colleagues? Are the provinces going to believe in free trade? Is he going to move first to persuade the First Ministers of the provinces to eliminate some of the barriers between the free movement of people and goods across provincial borders? Is he going to suggest to them: "Buy Ontario, buy Alberta, achetez Quebec". Is that the tenor and mood of what he is trying to suggest in our relationship with the United States?
He says that he is going to put this on the agenda at the next meeting of First Ministers with himself in the month of November.
What questions are you going to put, I say through you, Mr. Speaker, on the agenda? Are you going to be discussing provincial procurement policies? Are you going to be discussing provincial subsidies? Are you going to be suggesting and discussing provincial incentives? These are very important questions, I believe, because we would like to know how the Government intends to meet the needs of provincial Governments in the trade talks.
I think, Sir, too, it is time to end the myth that free trade means unrestricted and unfettered trade in absolutely all areas. That would be tantamount to joining some sort of economic union with the United States and I do not believe that that position is supported by a majority of Canadians.
Canadians are concerned, Sir, in these negotiations launched today by the Prime Minister and his Government about our political independence. We are concerned about our cultural integrity. We are concerned about the independence of the economic decision-making process. I do not know whether it was deliberate but on page 5 of the Prime Minister's statement he neglected to recite that in his presentation to the House, and I read that paragraph. In the text are the following words: "We are not negotiating a customs union, a common market or any other economic arrangement which would affect our own independence or our relations with the rest of the world". I take that to be his position but he did not bring it forth in his presentation to the House. We would certainly be very, very loath to be part of any such customs union arrangement.
It is time to end the myth that free trade means unrestricted and unfettered trade in absolutely all areas. Liberals have always supported freer trade.

The Liberals and the Liberal Party have always supported the liberalisation of trade relations, that is, a reduction in tariff and non-tariff barriers, but, as I have said many times before, never at the expense of our sovereignty, our cultural identity or our freedom of decision in economic matters. Any discussions on the subject must allow for the particular needs of our Canadian economy and society.

We will want to learn at the same time as the Government moves into these negotiations what its view is of some related questions. What will free trade or free trade arrangements or a freer trade arrangement mean in terms of the reconciliation of our stabilization policies? Our taxation policies? Our regional economic development policies? What will it mean in terms of the independence of the manoeuvres which the Canadian people have in living and governing themselves in their own way?
Mr. Speaker, there is a danger of being railroaded into a hasty decision which might later prove to be damaging to the Canadian interests. I must say that we on this side of the House or this quarter of the House, do not have much confidence in the Government's negotiating abilities. I watched the performance of the Prime Minister at the Quebec summit. The President wanted the abolition of the Foreign Investment Review Act. Yes, Sir, Mr. President, he got it. He wanted the elimination of the National Energy Program, yes, Sir, he got it.

We are asking whether we have any confidence in this team. Just as disturbing is the revelation last weekend. The United States invited four major powers, a group of five they like to call themselves, the United Kingdom, France, West Germany and Japan to a meeting called quite clandestinely. As a result of that meeting, there was an agreement among those five economic powers to work out ways to devalue the U.S. dollar. Was our Government informed? Was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) informed in advance? Was the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) informed? 1 want to know whether or not the Prime Minister was informed.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
At the Shamrock Summit, President Reagan said, "Brian, give me a call any time you have a problem". That has changed and is now, "Don't call me, we'll call you, Brian". He did not give us any warning at all.
September 26, 1985

There is no country more vulnerable to exchange movement in the American dollar than Canada. Billions of dollars cross our border every day. We have a mutual trade of $150 billion. Yet we were not informed of this. We are now entering a free trade negotiation with the United States while our potential partner did not have the decency or foresight to inform its future partner of an exchange rate movement, something which is frankly more important than the tariff levels to which I will turn in a moment. If that is the type of special relationship the Prime Minister now has with the President of the United States, it is certainly not the kind of special relationship that bears up in a matter of substance.
Tariff barriers have been reduced gradually and progressively throughout the negotiations on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. By 1987, 80 per cent of our trade with the United States will be free of tariffs and 15 per cent of our trade will be subject to tariffs of 5 per cent or less. That means that 95 per cent of all Canadian goods moving across the American border is already subject to a maximum tariff of 5 per cent or is not subject to a tariff at all. Movements in the exchange rate are now more important than or equally as important as the remaining tariffs. It is the non-tariff barriers about which we must worry.
The key area for discussion and negotiation continues to be non-tariff barriers like subsidies, regulations and procurement policies. The non-tariff barriers in the United States are protected under a new guise. It is a political, economic and legal one. It can be harassment of all three kinds with the way the United States economy operates. We have to know the impact of these negotiations regarding non-tariff barriers on the various regions and sectors of Canada.
In order to eliminate those non-tariff barriers, procurement policies of the provinces and of the states and exports subsidies, only a new style of treaty will work. What will work is not an agreement but a treaty binding the federal and state Governments of the United States and the federal and provincial Governments of Canada. We should not allow pressure from the United States Government to force us to include certain items as non-tariff barriers in the discussions.
Washington has a new vocabulary. The people there like to call negotiations on trade negotiations for a level playing field. A level playing field is local vocabulary for a preoccupation with hidden and overt subsidies that foreign governments provide for exports. Americans and the Congress in particular equate subsidies to so-called unfair competition. There are a whole range of subsidies now subject to countervailing duties. Among those subsidies are subsidies that go right to the heart of the regional economic development policy of this country.
We want a full declaration from the Government indicating how it intends to treat the following items in its negotiations with the United States: social programs, health care, unemployment insurance, which has already been considered a subsidy by some in the United States, family allowances and pensions. What are we going to do about the independence and integrity of our cultural industries? What about the independence, strength and ownership of our financial industries?
Statements by Ministers
What about agricultural support? What about the Canadian Wheat Board? What about all the marketing boards? What about the initial payment under the Wheat Board, something which has been considered by the United States to be a hidden subsidy? What about the auto pact?
We take the view that the auto pact ought not to be included in these negotiations. We take the view that a special arrangement ought to be made for agriculture and that our cultural and financial industries should remain intact.
What about equalization payments? Those could be considered hidden subsidies open to countervail unless they are specifically included in an agreement. What about export incentives for industries in the provinces that have sales directed at the American market? There is a whole range of policies and programs which, in the words of the Parliamentary Committee, are of fundamental importance to the maintenance of a distinctive Canadian identity or to keeping solemn commitments made to significant elements of Canadian society.
The issues to which I have referred should be spelled out very clearly at the outset. The Macdonald Commission has calculated the benefits of free trade but to date the Government has not provided us with an assessment of the costs by sector, by region, by industry and by worker. What will Canadian businesses and invididuals be asked to give up?
What about the footwear industry and the clothing industry? We all know that we are not going to get something for nothing through these negotiations. Is Canada going to lose entire industries as a result of the shift in economic activity? If so, which ones and where? What sort of adjustments to the system does the Government propose?
Has the Government explored all the alternatives to enhancing our economic performance? Some argue that the GATT process has already liberalized trade and that due to the complexity of our trading relationship with the United States, that process is the most effective way to increase our trade levels with the United States and other countries. Should we not, as the committee recommends, be concentrating first on settling existing irritants to trade with the United States, opening up informal discussions and setting up the parameters of these discussions with the United States? Should we not be listing the elements affected? Interprovincial trade needs to be examined and impediments removed.
What would be the impact of these negotiations on our other trading partners? Have we explored how Japan, the Third World and the European Economic Community will react? What will be the impact on Canadian jobs, regions, transitional programs and the full-employment strategy of the Government?
We have always encouraged the Government of Canada to seek ways to enhance our trade, not only with the United States but with all countries, through an effective trade strategy. We have encouraged the Government to improve our access to foreign markets. However, a debate such as this must be an open and public one and, in our view, it must precede any formal negotiations with the United States.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the agreement to your suggestion that has come from both sides of the House but I will try to stick closer to what I understand the rules to be which is that I will make a statement of about the same length as the one made on the other side of the House.
Let me begin by saying, not entirely facetiously, that I found this nationalist-oriented speech coming from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to be very strange coming as it did from a man who not very many months ago attacked the National Energy Program. Having made that point, I would like to say that, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) knows full well and as the Leader of the Opposition addressed in the substance of his comments, what we are talking about here is the very future of our nation. There can be nothing more important in the life of this Parliament than the subject matter the Prime Minister has introduced today.
I would say to the Prime Minister that when I read the brief document, I was alarmed, and I am speaking frankly. Knowing something about Canadian history, I know that it was the first Leader of the Conservative Party, the first Prime Minister of Canada, who gave this nation a national policy. With the advantage of 20/20 hindsight, I did not agree with all the details of that policy. However, with what I did agree as a Canadian was a sense of nationhood and a sense of commitment which went against the prevailing continentalism which existed south of the border and in parts of this land which said that we had to do certain things to build this nation on our own. He developed what he called a national policy which provided the foundation for this nation.
About three decades ago, another Conservative Leader, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, made one of the finest speeches I have ever read. As a matter of fact, it was a speech he gave in Saskatchewan where he spoke as a passionate Canadian nationalist and warned of the dangers of continentalism. It was not because he was anti-American. I hope in this debate we can avoid those caricature-type arguments. He made a passionate speech warning against the need to preserve certain
Canadian institutions, including economic ones, and traditional patterns of behaviour which we had built up here so that we would remain independent as a nation.
I wish to say to the Prime Minister that if he looks carefully at some of the key clauses he has included in his statement that what we have at this stage in the approach the Prime Minister is taking with the United States is a premature step of profoundly historical significance which will result, if it is carried out to its conclusion, not only in the ignoring of the warning of John Diefenbaker but the abandonment of the vision of John A. Macdonald.
Because I say that with seriousness I wish to express my concerns now. First, I wish to say that my Party across the nation, and Members from all sides of the House, would agree with the following assumptions as Canadians that we should be holding to at this point. We should begin by saying that anything we do in the economic domain of significance would involve our great neighbour to the south, the United States. We know that $150 billion of trade is involved between our two nations. We know that any sensible economic development in this country, expansion of jobs, and growth is inextricably linked to relationships with the United States. That is a given. Beyond that, it will involve the expansion of economic relationships and growth for both nations in terms of economic growth.
I also take it as a given that when we approach our American friends and neighbours we will do so without allusions. I hope we will negotiate not out of spirit of animosity but out of a spirit of tough-minded friendship, if I can put it that way, in the full knowledge that we have to look after our interests as politicians, which is what we are elected to do, just as American politicians have to look after their interests. When we negotiate we want something fair for both sides. There are a number of examples of this. I happen to come from an automotive community. I can cite that in picking up an argument which the Prime Minister has made that what he is proposing is to be consistent not only with the good of Canadians but with the good of the Third World. He made reference to the fact that what we do should be consistent with GATT. One of the interesting features of the automotive agreement is that not only did it expand trade on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border, and provide more jobs on both sides of the border, but from a Canadian point of view it was multilateral and applied to other nations, third and fourth nations. In that sense, it had a global perspective.
I say to the Prime Minister: Beware of our American friends, those tough bargainers, because when the Americans signed that agreement it was bilateral, which was not accidental. The Americans knew full well that the automotive industry on this continent is owned and controlled in the United States. They were prepared to enter into an agreement with us. It was mutually beneficial but they were thinking beyond that. They thought they made real gains, which is why they signed it. We thought we could make gains, which is why we signed it. I repeat, it was multilateral for us but bilateral for them.
September 26, 1985

There were important safeguards in it which recognized the economic reality that we are one-tenth as powerful as the United States, not because we are timed, backward looking or reserved, but simply because it is the most dominant economic power in the world, originally stronger in resources over-all, they would argue, and stronger in population. We have done well as a nation, very well indeed, with a smaller population. However, we should have no illusions about the strength of the Americans.
Any relationship we enter into with the United States ought to be one of seeing an expanded pie, if you like, for both, in the economic domain and elsewhere. As I said not long ago, what we must ensure, not because they are mean, vindictive or malicious, but simply because they are tough, competitive and pretty successful, is that when the elephant and the beaver sit down to eat this pie together that the elephant, inadvertently or not, does not unfold its trunk, pick up the pie and go home with it.
The key point we have to keep in mind is that we are dealing with a powerful neighbour. I say to the Prime Minister that 1 am concerned about the naivety, although I am not sure that is the right word, but the hastiness with which the Government is now committing itself to negotiations. The Prime Minister's words are important in this. He said that the Government has committed itself to negotiations. The Prime Minister had a conversation today with the President of the United States. He said that official negotiations are now getting under way.
If one considers the options, and I do not want to abuse the House in terms of time, they are really two-fold. We could do what the Government has now recommended, which is to enter into negotiations and follow the path which the Prime Minister has laid out. It cannot be any clearer than the words in his statement when he said that we seek to negotiate the broadest possible package of mutually-beneficial reductions in tariff and non-tariff barriers between our two countries. Economically, that is pretty specific with respect to what he has in mind. I will come to the implications for our institutions and the relationships to that type of economic goal in a moment.
We could have done what the Prime Minister has announced with, I take for granted, the support of his caucus, which is to embark on that path right away. Or we could have taken another approach. We could have said that there are specific and real problems of Canadians, as there are of Americans, but beginning on our side we could say that there are certain obstacles. Not long ago I was in Atlantic Canada at a time when a decision came down in the United States which, in part, responded to arguments which said that the unemployment insurance plan in Canada constituted a subsidy for the Canadian fishery and, therefore, argumentation was made that that type of program, by implication, should not exist in Canada if we are to really have a free trade arrangement. Countervailing steps are being taken.
We have problems in the fishery on the East Coast. Our fishermen thought they had access to a U.S. market which is now taking countervailing action. We should negotiate and talk about that problem.

The lumber export business in Canada is running into countervailing action, not just on the West Coast but everywhere across the country. Our hog producers in Quebec-

Mr. Speaker, we fully support the recent changes in immigration policy resulting from a court decision requiring oral hearings for refugees and immigrants. This was long overdue and it is a just and sensible decision. However, as I indicated this morning, as a result there has been a considerable increase in the number of appeals and a backlog has developed which means long delays for both refugees and sponsors of immigrants who requested and were refused admission to Canada. Unfortunately, our critic on immigration, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), was not able to be here today but I would like to quote from a press release of his dated April 23. He said:
"Eight years is long enough for a refugee to wait in limbo," said Dan Heap, M.P., NDP critic on Immigration. Mr. Heap demanded that the Minister of Employment & Immigration take action right away to end the waiting for 20,000 refugee claimants in Canada.
"The Supreme Court said on April 4, 1985 that they are all entitled to a hearing," said Mr. Heap, who represents many refugees and immigrants in his riding, Spadina.
Mr. Heap said that the figure of 20,000 includes people who could have been landed already, and do not need to be added to the backlog.
"For example," said Mr. Heap, a mother whose husband was killed and children persecuted for their politics back home ought to be landed on humanitarian grounds. Others with strong family ties in Canada ought to be admitted on humanitarian grounds, he suggested, as well as those who come from war zones. Besides, Mr. Heap pointed out, there are genuine refugee claimants who

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
give clear evidence that they have already been persecuted, but are being held back by red tape.
"Why do the officials take so many months just to type up the transcript of the claimant's statement under oath for the Refugee Status Advisory Committee to read?" Mr. Heap asked. "And if they really want to reduce the backlog and save time, why do they put people unnecessarily into the refugee stream?"
We have concerns in this regard, Mr. Speaker. We are particularly concerned about the piecemal approach being used in this Bill. This is rather strange because last June the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said:
A piecemeal approach could have very negative results for refugees who really need our help.
However, we have here a piecemeal Bill. Increasing the size of the Immigration Appeal Board from 18 members to 50 will not necessarily deal with the backlog of cases more effectively. It is important that appointees to this Board be carefully selected for their expertise, experience and sensitivity to the situation of immigrants, particularly refugees. Too often in the past appointees to the Board have been former immigration officials who, despite being well-intentioned, I am sure, have been really indoctrinated in bureaucratic procedures. It has usually been their job in the past to decide why these applicants are not eligible to stay in Canada. They often had to refuse applicants so they are hardly likely to be particularly sensitive on the other side and act as advocates on behalf of the applicants during an appeal. The process allows for bureaucratic input in the early stages, and having former officials of the Department on the IAB hardly gives a different perspective, one which is more objective and sympathetic toward the appellant. That is why we ask the Minister to be careful in appointing former bureaucrats to the Board. It is most important that appointees to the Board be from varying backgrounds, people who can be objective but who also have a particular sensitivity toward the immigrant and his or her family.
We have concerns that the expanded Board will apparently deal with refugee claims and appeals as well as other immigration cases which are often quite different in nature. Churches, community groups and lawyers have expressed concern that the IAB in the past has had very little experience and a very poor track record in recognizing genuine refugees. We are concerned about that in the present as well, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, we feel there should be a separate Board dealing specifically with refugee cases. This was recommended in the Plaut report on refugee redetermination published last June. This is most important. There are many circumstances which contribute to creating political refugees and these have been defined by the UN. However, I must say that in some cases I have been involved in as a Member of Parliament there have been times when the Board and this country appear to be much more rigid in their interpretation than is the UN. We know that most of these people cannot return to their homes and it is important that they have a genuine and sympathetic hearing.
I would like to read from some notes of my colleague referring to comments by church and community groups, as
well as immigration lawyers, who have a great deal of experience in this area. They have for years demanded an oral hearing. Now that the Supreme Court in the Singh case, assisted by the Canadian Council of Churches, has declared that refugees have the right to be heard directly by those who decide their fate, there is strong insistence that the hearing process not be watered down. They fear this move would enhance the power of a bureaucracy which has been hostile to refugee immigrants in Canada, and would result in many genuine refugees being deported to a dangerous situation in their home countries. There is a better way. The Standing Conference of Canadian Organizations Concerned for Refugees, which is composed of about 70 groups and which predicted eight years ago that our refugee claim process was unjust and would fail, has been vindicated by the Supreme Court. It has proposed an alternative way to address the backlog. They point out that the Minister and several successive Ministers could have made better use of the Minister's power under the legislation to create special measures or special programs for designated groups. For example, Iranians who arrived last year were not told by immigration officers that Canada has a special program for Iranians. Basically Canada does not send Iranians back to Iran. These people were manoeuvred into claiming refugee status which requires a case-by-case examination on a narrow legal basis and which takes much more time and of course costs more than the special program. It is estimated by a well-informed source that if all the refugee claimants who should have been directed to the special programs, plus the Guyanese who ought to have one, were taken out of the refugee stream, the backlog would be reduced to a quarter of its present size. Therefore that group, at a recent consultation in Toronto, asked that the Minister declare a special humanitarian program for all those caught in this bureaucratic jungle as of April 4, 1984.
It is worth noting that Rabbi Plaut, in his report on refugee redetermination in Canada, considers that this humanitarian and compassionate system of special programs has been too little used and should be used now. We ask the Minister to consider this as a better alternative for preventing the backlog which he often faces and which this Bill is directed to in a rather expedient way.
We were pleased this morning to hear the Minister clarify one of our very strong concerns with this Bill in that he has decided to amend the Bill to re-establish a panel of three persons who will hear appeals by sponsors to bring in their relatives as permanent residents. The original proposal contained in this Bill was to have a quorum of one person. In our view that would not be an objective appeal procedure. One person can only speak for himself or herself and that results in a very subjective evaluation. Three people give a balance and provide more expertise which can be shared in a final decision.
We also support Clause 6 which provides a simpler appeal process, provided that there is a three-person board to hear the appeal. It is a good thing that permanent residents will now have the same right as Canadian citizens to appeal the rejec-

tion of a sponsorship application of a relative. Many of us who deal with many immigration cases in our ridings find it very heartbreaking when a person who is a landed immigrant, but not yet a citizen, is unable to use the appeal procedure which is available to his next door neighbour who has just completed citizenship. We agree with the changes in this regard. There must be a fair and impartial hearing process and we, therefore, feel very strongly that there must be three people.
The NDP is very concerned that piecemeal steps are being taken through Bill C-55 and that this ignores the general recommendations of the Plaut proposal which we support. I would like to again quote our immigration critic who said in June:
Rabbi Plaut has given a just, quick and inexpensive proposal for 13,800 people in Canada.
The Member for Spadina called on the Minister of Employment and Immigration to use Rabbi Plaut's proposal. The Supreme Court said that none of the 13,800 people claiming refugee status in Canada should be deported without first having a chance to meet face-to-face, in an oral hearing, with those who decide their fate. However, he pointed out that there are many, in fact the majority, who deserve to be allowed to stay even without a hearing. Many of these come from countries such as Afghanistan, Iran, El Salvador, or Sri Lanka, to which Canada does not force people to return. These could all be issued Minister's permits to stay, except those already under deportation order. They could be allowed to go briefly to the United States to be readmitted to Canada. In Vancouver we call this the "Seattle shuffle". Many of these people have come from countries torn by war or racial violence and have families .here to help them settle. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have such a large audience for my grand finale. I hope they are all going to listen very intently. As I was saying when I was somewhat distracted by the bells, there is a great need for an over-all review and a revamping of our immigration policy and procedures in Canada. Many of us who have dealt with immigration cases have very special concerns which arrive from them and indicate a need for policy change. I would like to mention several examples which illustrate problems that I hope the Minister will explore and which should have been considered
Immigration Act, 1976
in a broader immigration Bill. Some of these involve attitudi-nal changes as well.
The Minister stated this morning that he wants to encourage family immigration. We all favour this goal, but we wish that the Government really meant it. While the Minister extols family immigration, there is no question that the policy of the Government has gone in the opposite direction. Family reunification is being curtailed by the Government in favour of a "buy your way into Canada" policy. Entrepreneurs are given priority over ordinary workers and families. An elite moneyed class is being favoured by the Conservative Government. I suppose the Government hopes these people will vote Conservative once they get here. It is necessary to have at least $5,000 of capital, and in many cases much more, in order to come to Canada. There is no guarantee at all that the entrepreneurs who come will create additional jobs.
We do not oppose business people coming to Canada if it will add to jobs, but we think that the priority in this regard is unfair. Many families have been waiting for years to bring remaining relatives to Canada. Many of these relatives are alone. I know of many young women who have been left in countries where it is really forbidden for women to be separated from their extended families. These young women cannot come into Canada because they are over the age of 21. We feel that there is considerable evidence and a long history of immigrants and sponsors being very responsible in caring for family members and ensuring that they are able to get housing and financial assistance and not become dependent on the Government. We should examine our priorities again in favour of family reunification.
Another issue is that of exploitation of immigrants by immigration lawyers and consultants. This has been raised frequently by my friend and colleague, the Member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). This area should be explored. Sponsors and prospective immigrants to Canada should be given information freely. They should be told their rights and given help with procedures. I think we should even have interpretation services available when needed. In particular, I think they should be told how to appeal. They should not have to go to a lawyer and pay a huge sum of money to have these fairly routine procedures carried out for them. They should be aware of how to use their Members of Parliament in circumstances where they are having difficulty and need extra help. Costly legal fees are often not necessary and sometimes the somewhat unethical practices of lawyers are exploiting people unnecessarily.
A third issue is that of domestics. We still discriminate against domestics, most of whom are women. When they come to Canada on work visas they have very few protections and very little chance of becoming landed immigrants. Today one of my colleagues gave me a letter which describes a very sad and unfair situation which discriminates against a domestic and her mentally retarded daughter. This woman had been in Canada for five years and had always worked at the same place as a domestic. She had a mentally retarded daughter whom she wanted to have join her. Her employers were willing

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
to accommodate them. She had a regular job. The Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded supported her request for a ministerial permit, but she was twice denied permission for her daughter to join her in Canada. I think that is discriminatory in several respects.
I am surprised that the new Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) was the latest one to refuse her daughter entry. I think his reasons, in the letter which I saw, were extremely weak. We should be changing our policies and procedures to provide much greater opportunity and protection for domestic workers who come to Canada.
There also seems to be a deliberate policy to discourage immigration from certain parts of the world. We have received repeated complaints and examples of this, particularly from India, Pakistan and Hong Kong. Today I was told about a Halifax doctor who brought his parents to Canada from Islamabad. His last remaining relative, his daughter, has been refused permission to come to this country, despite the fact that there is a written policy indicating that the last remaining relative should have special consideration to join the family. This family has also waited five months for its appeal to be considered.
We need to look at our immigration policy in respect of cases involving health problems which have been treated and are judged in a very inhumane way by Immigration officials. I can think of several where there was no danger to the health of other persons, where there was a chronic situation and where the family was willing to assume all financial responsibilities. One case involved two Vietnamese men. They were the last remaining sons; the whole family had settled in Canada. They were left in a refugee camp in Thailand. They had a history of mental illness, but health officials at the refugee camp said that it was due to the stress of camp life and of not being reunited with their family. These medical authorities felt that they should be reunited with their families and that their health problem was not serious. They were refused permission to join their family, and that is still the case.
I am particularly concerned about the problems facing women who want to immigrate to Canada and those who have already come here with their husbands. I ask the Minister to give special attention to these areas because he is also the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. Women are still treated as spouses; they are not treated as individuals with rights of their own. When they come to Canada with their families and their husbands, they are treated as spouses. The husband is the individual who applies, gets the points and is recognized by the Department of Immigration. This results in a very insecure situation for women. They are really here as dependents and are second-class citizens. Often such women remain in very damaging marital situations once they have come here because they have no real rights, no financial security, no alternatives, and they fear deportation.
Another example is men who have arranged for women to come to Canada on the promise of marriage. We know of
many examples where they bring over women and the immigration papers indicate that it is with the prospect of marriage or that they are fiancees. They get them here and then they do not marry them. They are exploited, they have no protection of security. 1 recall the slave trade-and that is really what it is-in poor women from Third World countries through agencies both in Canada and Australia, in particular. Marriages have been arranged of poor women who are desperate to survive to unknown older men. There is a history of exploitation and a loss of rights.
We require a complete review of federal and provincial policies to provide a better integrated program for refugees and immigrants. There are times when people who have been here for some time, and their families, are destitute through no fault of their own. Who could have predicted the tremendous unemployment to which we have been subjected? This has affected some people who came to Canada years ago. Occasionally such people need social assistance. The instances are rare. Our population of immigrant families has a proud history of looking after their own. They do not apply for outside help unless there is absolutely no other way of surviving. We need to look at that matter and at providing more co-ordination on the part of the federal Government and provincial Governments in the area of social assistance.
I am particularly concerned about inland refugees from Latin American countries. In Vancouver, they have been lining up at food banks because they are not given the same kind of consideration when attempting to receive refugee status as the Poles, for example. There are long delays. Many women with children cannot feed their children-they have no money, they are ineligible for social assistance, and they are destitute. Some arrangements should be made to provide them with social assistance during the waiting period.
In conclusion, I am sure there are many other concerns which have not been mentioned today. The point we are trying to make is that we should not be dealing with only a small part of the immigration scene through one Bill in an ad hoc way or in a piecemeal way. We should be introducing a more comprehensive immigration Bill to look at many items which have been substantiated. If the Minister looks at her own case-load of appeals made to her on humanitarian grounds, she will see similar cases indicating that a change in policy and often a change in attitude, on the part of Immigration officials are needed. We urge the Minister to amend the Bill to deal with our specific concerns and to work, along with all of us, toward a more just, equitable and positive immigration policy in general.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to have this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, on this memorable and historic day, after hearing the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announce that discussions will be held with the United States on the liberalization of trade relations.

Mr. Speaker, the procedure for claiming refugee status, which was implemented when the Act became effective in 1978, provides for two review levels. The first is the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, which sits in Ottawa and is responsible for evaluating the transcript of the interview under oath and informing the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) of its conclusions. The Minister then determines whether or not the claim is valid. If the claim is denied, the claimant may appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board. The decisions of the Board are subject to judicial review under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act.
Claimants who go through the whole process may be in Canada for more than three years. That is why an increasing number of people are coming to Canada for the sole purpose of claiming refugee status and thus perhaps having a chance of staying in this country permanently.
The sheer numbers have led to unacceptable delay in handing down decisions in the case of bona fide refugees. We are even unable to put claimants whose claims are not bona fide out of the country, even if their claims were obviously not valid from the start.
Pending a decision on their claims, these people have no status in Canada. We find them in our largest urban centres, where they barely manage to survive. They are not eligible for federal assistance, and access to provincial welfare programs is limited in their case.
Unfortunately, there are many such people without status in Canada, and there is also a lack of staff to conduct investigations. This means we have a class of people who want to become Canadians, who are living in a state of anxiety, who cannot buy a house, who cannot plan for the future, cannot get married, cannot raise a family because they do not know what tomorrow will bring since they are not sure they will be allowed to stay in this country.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, something should be done for all those people.
In April 1984 Rabbi Gunther Plaut was commissioned to hold consultations and make recommendations on a new refugee status recognition system, and that will eventually lead to amendments to the Act. His report was released last June and, later on in this session, Parliament will be asked to consider legislative provisions based on that report.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has already launched public consultations which will pave the way for the formulation of a new application review system. Once it has received Cabinet approval, it will be necessary to amend the Immigration Act. Those consultations are a prerequisite because we must find some kind of balance between administrative expedients and outright protection for bona fide refugees who will be helped by the many Canadian organizations which take them under their wings.
Immigration Act, 1976
For the time being, however, we need a strategy designed to reduce the current backlog of applications so as to alleviate the difficulties experienced by refugees and make sure the undue delays do not create a de facto immigrant category. That is why new resources are needed at every stage of the existing system, and the Act must be amended to make the Immigration Appeal Board rules more flexible. That is the only way the Immigration Appeal Board will be able to tackle the ever growing number of cases it must deal with once they have gone through the system's preliminary stages.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-55 does not deal only with refugee status recognition, but with appeals as well. Certain figures might interest you. We think that this year the Appeal Board will be called upon to render 1,200 decisions on sponsorship applications. It is also expected to render 600 more decisions in other types of cases such as deportations, motions, applications for release in cases of deportation orders, and so on. With respect to refugee status recognition, we are talking about at least 2,870 decisions. In other words, to a large extent this increase applies as well to the Board's appeal caseload, not only to the number of refugees.
Unless we act soon the refugee status application problem will create personal hardships. Since it is impossible in the near future to adopt wide-ranging amendments to come to grips with the basic problem, it becomes necessary to implement transitional measures indicating that Parliament is fully aware of humanitarian requirements, that it intends to take steps to carry out fully the Supreme Court decision to which the Minister has already referred, and that it is committed to establish a long term amendment program designed to cope with current difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that we make fundamental changes in the refugee status recognition system. That is not the purpose of the Bill before us today. Actually it is our response to the most pressing human needs, in other words our way to deal with the growing backlog of all IAB cases, not only those which have to do with refugee status recognition applications. That is inherent in Canada's humanitarian traditions. I therefore urge all Hon. Members on either side of the House to support Bill C-55.
Are there any questions or comments? If there are no questions, we will resume debate. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).

Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings that I enter this debate because it is one that requires much thoughtful analysis of the Bill before us and which I must say, having analyzed its clauses, is one that leaves me wondering about what the intent of the Government is with respect to changing the Immigration Act.

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
I will explain briefly what I mean. The Government has had one year's time to prepare a set of amendments of what is, in my view and I am sure in yours, Mr. Speaker, one of the most important social policy pieces of legislation that we have, namely, how to regulate the arrival of people who decide to settle in Canada. People from all parts of the world look on Canada as a very desirable country. People who can travel and wish to emigrate here like to obtain the highly desired landed immigrant visa and the number of people who knock on our door is immense. That number is augmented by the fact that there are people who, for political reasons, have decided to come to Canada as visitors and then seek landed immigrant status here.
There are other situations that cannot be defined in the first and second category that I just mentioned. There are people who come here by various illegal means but who, pushed by desperate economic conditions in their homeland, made a decision and chose Canada as a land for themselves and their families. The numbers in this latter category have swelled.
We all looked with anticipation and anxiety at the arrival of Bill C-55 hoping to find in it some answers that would resolve a big problem, give us a sense of direction telling the world that we are coming to grips not only with the immense backlogs of applicants but also the problems in the existing legislation which have emerged because those problems were not foreseen because of changing times.
As we look at the law, we find that one has to arrive at a rather disappointing conclusion even if one approaches it with an open mind. Community groups and volunteer groups have made representations over the past year with regard to improving the law. In addition to that we have had a report by Rabbi Gunther Plaut of Toronto. It attempted to design a new approach for the Government, a new mechanism, to resolve the movement of refugees. Therefore input has been considerable. At the other end of the spectrum, at the moment of producing the Bill, we do not find substance or inspiration accompanying these submissions made to the Government by both the immigrant community groups and the Plaut report. Therefore, what we have here before us, I regret to conclude, is an effort that can only be described as a stopgap measure. It attempts to accelerate the existing mechanism of processing people who want to become landed immigrants. Therefore we find in Sections 1, 2 and 3 the enlargement of the Appeal Board to 15 and the number of vice-chairmen going from five to 13 and other measures that are intended to facilitate the functioning of that specific Immigration Appeal Board.
To make the Bill a little bit more attractive, I suppose, there is also a measure of granting the right of appeal to landed immigrants, to permanent residents, a right that exists so far only for Canadian citizens. But the substance that is required at this stage is missing because the manner and the fairness and the quality of the decision-making process that applies so far as experienced by those who are in charge of processing people who are waiting for a landed immigrant status will not
be changed. In other words, the quality of the process will not be affected by this Bill and that is the regrettable part.
We, of course, in the Liberal Party will press in committee beyond this stage of debate here in the House. We will press for amendments. We hope that the Minister will approach the whole subject in committee with an open mind and accept a number of proposals that are definitely intended to improve the quality of the Bill. However, there is only so much that can be done within the framework of this piece of legislation which unfortunately is narrow and does not incorporate the good stuff, the good advice, the well thought out ideas that, as I said, have been produced by individuals and by groups in the year past.
Any discussion on the Immigration Act must say something about certain situations, namely the fact that at the present time there are delays that go into a considerable number of years in the processing of orders in council. The landing process, in other words, for people who are waiting for their order in council is extremely long and it causes a number of hardships on the economic well-being of the families affected. The practice of issuing a social insurance number starting with the number nine to those who are approved but have not been finally landed is causing hardships for those who seek employment. They find it extremely difficult to convince employers to hire them.
In addition to delays there is the question of insensitivity on the part of officials in certain situations. There is, for instance, the case of a single mother with children who has been waiting for permission to come to Canada. She is a refugee in a camp in Austria, having fled Czechoslovakia but our officials feel she should not be assisted in coming over to join her sister who has been a Canadian citizen for many years because of a court order that has been issued in her country of origin, namely Czechoslovakia.
Here is a person who is most eager and ready to move to Canada and lives under very stressful conditions and yet there does not seem to be that sensitivity on the part of our officials that ought to accompany the processing of such an application.
There is in the present legislation, and probably it was an oversight in past legislation, a situation that affects adolescents between the ages of 13 and 18 who cannot be adopted and for whom there is no provision in the law for anyone to adopt them while they are visiting here in Canada, even when there is a family willing to adopt them. There is in other words a gap of age between that of 13 and 18 which negatively affects young people. That is a case that was widely publicized a few weeks ago in Alberta. It is only suitable that in International Youth Year we would look at this Bill in the hope of finding some of the answers that could only be the result of the experience of the last few years having seen what the shortcomings are of the existing piece of legislation.
The present piece of legislation that is before us today deals mostly with Immigration Appeal Board methods but it is called the Immigration Act. I submit to you that it lacks compassion in not bringing forward some of the changes that I am sure the Department is capable of advancing and suggest-
September 26, 1985

ing to the Minister so that this Bill would be enhanced and enriched and improved in its quality. I would hope that once we are beyond this stage in committee the Minister will want to take the initiative himself and come to committee or, through the offices of the Parliamentary Secretary, bring to committee a number of amendments that flow from the experience in recent years and go beyond the approach that is outlined in this Bill.
We find it, as a Bill, a disappointing piece. It is true that there is, as I said, an enlargement of the Board which of course has to take place in order to process more readily and it is true that it has a measure that will give landed immigrants and residents the right to appeal. We will support those measures. We would like very much to move the debate beyond that and urge the Government to give the whole matter the broader approach and the broader outlook that this Bill is badly missing. When I gave the examples on delays and insensitivities or the example of the young people between the ages of 13 and 18 who fall between two stools and cannot be dealt with under the present legislation, I did that with the limited knowledge that I have of the subject only to illustrate a certain situation with some examples because it does not happen very often that there is legislative time to bring forwad a Bill to amend the Immigration Act. When it happens I submit it would be desirable from the point of view of everyone who feels that immigration is such an important and delicate aspect of Canada's growth and expansion that it should be as comprehensive as possible.
Faced with that dilemma of Bill C-55 we would like to seek some indication by the Government that this is not the end of it, that this is just a preliminary Bill that the Government is examining perhaps in greater depth as it should, the report by Rabbi Plaut, that it is examining the submissions made by citizens' groups and that it is engaging in that kind of constructive, productive, consultative work that eventually leads to legislation flowing from this kind of consultation. Then we will be able to see the promises translated into legislative action. Unfortunately, this Bill does not do that. It is a mechanical Bill which focuses on removing a bottleneck which definitely exists and it somehow removes the pressure to introduce reform to a system which evidently needs to be reformed. This is what troubles us on this side of the House because as we all know, every initiative in life has its own cycle and once it has served its purpose, it must be replaced by another.
It is now time for reform. We have been given the advice of those who are the practitioners in the field in a number of ways but that has not been translated into action through this Bill. That is why we are urging the Minister and the Government to make up for what this Bill does not contain. Our criticism is addressed at the absence of amendments of a practical nature affecting certain age groups and certain situations. On the basis of its statistics and the lessons learned in preceding years, I am sure the Department could produce such legislation.
Immigration Act, 1976
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that legislation is improved by looking at how an existing law as we know it has performed and served us over the years. Since we are all frail human beings, we cannot produce perfect laws but we can improve the existing laws because we have tested them. That is the essence of the approach I am trying to outline this afternoon.
At the end of this debate, the Minister may want to enlighten us as to his stand on the following question: is this the end of this initiative or is this Bill one that will be followed by a more comprehensive Bill based upon a reformed set of criteria? If that is the case, we should know about it. We should know about it now because it will guide us when we go to committee where we will definitely by proposing amendments based on the observations that we have made in the course of this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I was a little disturbed by the degree of knowledge which seems to be percolating in the two opposition Parties. The Standing Committee which I have the honour to chair has held over 40 hearings on immigration matters since January and has already brought forward three substantial reports. We began an examination of the Plaut Report on Tuesday. The committee will meet again today at six o'clock to hear witnesses from the Bar Association, Sikh societies, umbrella groups and Rabbi Plaut himself. We will hear all of those witnesses between now and October 9.
The Hon. Member asked a question of the Minister in the Minister's absence. The committee is functioning very closely with the Minister and Members of all three Parties. I think there were consultations with the Minister yesterday and we heard representations from all three Parties. The very clear-cut timetable for the Standing Committee is to try to conclude its hearings by the middle of October and submit representations by the end of October so that some of the major changes relating to the Plaut Report will hopefully be in place by Christmas.
I have a question for the Hon. Member who just spoke. He is a senior member of his caucus and acknowledges that there is a bottleneck in the system. He did not say so, but I suspect he knows, as do most Members of the House, that that bottleneck is extremely hard on people who are caught in it. They find themselves in very difficult circumstances. The Hon. Member is also aware that the Government brought this Bill before the House in June and tried mightily to get it passed by the end of June so that those additional resources could be put in place and the bottleneck could open up. We are dealing with human lives here.
Is the Member signalling this Chamber that the senior members of the Liberal Party of Canada who serve in this Chamber intend to keep the bottleneck intact just because the Bill does not deal with everything in the universe of immigration? Are they really going to dig in their heels and filibuster to the point where we cannot begin to clear up the bottleneck?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is conjuring up notions that he seems to perceive can be drawn from my intervention. He makes a lot of

Immigration Act, 1976
the fact that the Bill was introduced in June 1985. This Bill, short as it is, and with the work that had been done before September 1984, could have been tabled in the House in November or at the latest December 1984. There was no need to wait until June 1985 to produce this kind of legislation. It is a three-page mechanical Bill. Knowledge of this matter was already available before the September election. If there was a real concern with bottlenecks-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: That's exactly right, and for five years before.

If there was a concern with a bottleneck on the part of the so-called Progressive Conservative party, it could have introduced this legislation in late 1984.
Certainly we are not here to engage in delaying tactics. We have explained our position in principle. We feel that the fundamentals are missing from this Bill. We see that this Bill does have some mechanical value because it will facilitate an existing process. However, I must repeat, in all fairness to the Hon. Member, that this approach will not improve the fairness with which we handle the immigration process at the present time. We are not incorporating the substantial criteria advanced by the Plaut Report some time ago.

Mr. Speaker, I find the paranoia of the Hon. Member for Calgary West on this particular question to be unseemly and certainly unjustified. I am new to this House but I certainly know the tactics which have been used by previous Governments. Legislation is brought in immediately prior to a summer recess and then the Government of the day indicates that it would have passed the legislation if it had co-operation from Opposition Parties. I know the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is familiar with that provision because he sat in opposition for a number of years and exactly the same charges were levied at him. I wish that since people voted for change on September 4 that we would not have to hear the same tired type of political rhetoric coming from the Government. The Hon. Member for Calgary West perhaps might more appropriately have commented on the fact that when the Hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was in Government, as the Minister responsible in this particular area, concerning himself with matters of multiculturalism, there was not pressure which yielded action within the Liberal Government to ensure there was no backlog of refugee cases, and to ensure that there was no backlog before the Immigration Appeal Board, and that the matters which had become so evident since the 1976 changes in the Act were, in fact, acted upon. I find it a bit hypocritical for the Liberal Party critic to criticize the Government now when, in fact, the Liberals had the opportunity to make these changes, and yet they left a plateful of unfinished business to the Conservatives.
I find it equally intolerable that the new Governemnt after one year should say: "We just arrived. We have not had time." The Government has had a year to show that it is prepared to make some decisive changes. Rather than do that we are presented with a makeshift Bill which is inadequate, which I
will comment on shortly. It is a Bill with no guarantee that there will be a real determination to stop this totally inhumane backlog which requires people to wait for years upon years before they know whether their status in Canada can be determined or not.
