The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak on Bill C-55. Our Party's critic on immigration, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), regrets not being here today. The reason he is not here today is because, to put it mildly, we are a bit confused by the Government's management of House business. We have had to predict what will come next on a minute-by-minute basis. It is somewhat like predicting who will be in the Cabinet tomorrow, which one has to go on a minute-by-minute basis.
In my response a moment ago during the period for questions and comments, I said these changes to relieve the backlog of appeals on immigration could and should have been made a long time ago. I find the whole process by which refugee appeals were being considered merely on the transcripts and the quality of the judgments being made by the officers appointed to hear that particular question under the Minister's jurisdiction, and also by the Immigration Appeal Board, left a great deal to be desired. I say that because I think a great
September 26, 1985

many Canadians felt that we as Canadians are fortunate in the world and that we should be a model with respect to reaching out and welcoming into our country persons who are refugees. From time to time we have done this, for example, in the case of Asians from Uganda and in the case of the Vietnamese. In those cases our record was not perfect, but it was not bad either. In other instances, however, with respect to refugees from Chile and refugees from Central America our record has been far less than perfect. There are some 13,500 refugees who are backed up in the system right now and whose appeals, as the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis) said a minute ago, are taking up to three years to be heard. In many cases they are held up not because of waiting for appeals to the Immigration Appeal Board but because of the prior process which is entirely within the Minister's discretion.
We in our Party are concerned about this Bill for two reasons. We are concerned because we feel it is prejudging recommendations made by the Plaut Commission Report, recommendations which, as the Hon. Member who spoke a few moments ago indicated, are now under active consideration by the committee of the House which looks into matters of immigration. In fact, there will be a report coming down shortly with respect to where we should go with the Plaut Report.
We feel that the proposal to take refugee appeals away from the Immigration Appeal Board makes a great deal of sense. Under those circumstances, the stopgap procedures proposed in the Bill before us just do not make an awful lot of sense. Why beef up the Immigration Appeal Board in order to deal with refugee appeals if, in fact, it is to be judged within another month or two that the policy will be to take those refugee appeals away from the Immigration Appeal Board entirely and establish an entirely separate tribunal, as proposed in the Plaut Report? For that matter, why beef up either tribunal if, in fact, the Government comes to the view, as I think it should have already, that the problem is not just at the end of the pipeline but with the number of cases which are being put into the pipeline?
Governmental policy under the previous Government, and I believe this Government as well, is that this Government will not turn people away and make them go back to their native countries if they come from such strife-torn countries as Afghanistan, certain countries in Central America or certain countries behind the Iron Curtain in the Soviet bloc, particularly the satellite Soviet countries. Under those circumstances, the failure of the new Ministry to take enough time to focus on this particular question, to decide that special measures are needed, is something which should have been done by the old Ministry. However, the new Ministry is new and not bound by the precedents of the past. It does not have to take as a given every word of advice it receives from the civil servants. In fact, it has an opportunity to bring a fresh approach to the situation. As I said a moment ago, that is what I believe Canadians voted for in the election of September 4.
My Party has been accused of being in coalition with the new Government of Ontario, the Liberal Government. That is
Immigration Act, 1976
not true. However, we have entered into an accord on a number of areas of policy which has, if nothing else, given an agenda for action to the new Government in Ontario. I am glad that after 40-odd years of Conservative Government, which deserved to be defeated, that the agenda for action which was laid down by the New Democrats is, in fact, being followed and that over the course of the last two or three months under Mr. Peterson's Government there is evidence of crisp decision making. A decision has been taken to seize the reins of power and to do something with them.
The federal Government has been elected with an enormous majority in terms of the House of Commons. It seems to be rapidly frittering away its grip on power even more quickly than the Diefenbaker Government did after its monumental victory of 1958.
As one commentator said, yesterday was Black Wednesday for this Government. We all know that when those types of affairs occur, when the competence of the Government is clearly not there, when the Government is engaged in firefighting and in dealing with the crisis of the day, that longer-term problems cannot be attended to. As early as the second year of this Government, it no longer appears to have the ability to stand back from the problems in order to come up with solutions and to show the courage, determination and political will to actually implement them.
The previous speaker suggested that if this Bill was needed as a stopgap that it could have been brought in as early as January or February in conjunction with the statement that as soon as the Plaut Report was released the Government would ask for advice of the committee which deals with matters of immigration and would then bring in its program immediately thereafter. Instead, the publication of the Plaut Report was delayed. We now have a stopgap decision taken at this time and no indication that the Government will have any capacity to take a fresh look during the three or four-year life of this Parliament, if Parliament even lasts that long.
I would like to come back to the specific measures in the Bill, apart from the measure which allows landed immigrants in Canada to have the same status as Canadian citizens in serving as sponsors, which our Party welcomes. The major feature of this Bill is to provide for an expansion of the Immigration Appeal Board. Its current maximum number is 18. The Chairperson of the Board told the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration in the spring that the board would be expanded by seven members by September 1. I guess that provision will have to wait since the Government did not get the Bill through in June. It will be expanded by another eight members by the end of the year, almost a doubling in size from 18 to 35. Subsequently, a further 15 members will be added to bring the membership up to 50, if that numerical increase is warranted. She suggested this is a short-term program and that the new members would be brought on for two-year terms. She suggested very strongly that people were effectively being asked to keep their hand in at teaching, the law or whatever profession or trade they had because they were only being taken on for two years and after
7074

September 26, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
two years it was easier to return to one's former line of work than if one took on a five-year term. This is a training program for inexperienced members of the appeal board who are to be there for a short term, and who are being informed that they will be there for a short term. Yet these people will be charged with the responsibility of just about tripling the rate at which the Immigration Appeal Board considers the appeals which are before it.
Any organization which expands that fast has problems in terms of its learning curve. It takes time before the new members learn how to handle the cases. The estimates, therefore, of the amount of time that cases are going to take to be heard are likely to be very optimistic. In addition to that, as the Minister and many spokespeople have acknowledged, the number of persons, legal counsel, immigration advisers and that kind of person, who are really qualified and able to represent appellants in this particular area, is very limited and, therefore, there will be tremendous strains on them from a tripling or quadrupling of the cases before the Immigration Appeal Board. Yet the Government's answer to the crisis is not in looking at ways to reduce the people waiting in the pipeline, as our Party has proposed. We propose ways to reduce by three quarters the number of people who might be appealing rejection of refugee status. However, instead of acting in that direction, Mr. Speaker, the Government decides to try to step up the work of the Immigration Appeal Board.
This Appeal Board is very costly, Mr. Speaker. I suppose the salary for the members is in the order of $35,000 to $50,000 a year. Perhaps it will be more if the Government hopes to acquire people with legal training and able to make a lawyer's income to come in and serve for a couple of years. That means that with 30 extra members, support staff, hearing space, hearing officers and all of the other trappings of the office, we are talking about a very major investment in terms of the cost of handling cases. Many of those cases, it seems to me, ought not to be there.
The former Government refused to give oral hearings to people applying for refugee status. In my opinion, the former Government also failed to look realistically, perhaps, at ways in which the law might be altered in order to try and differentiate between people who have a genuine claim, a realistic claim, to be considered for refugee status and, on the other hand, persons who are simply trying to abuse the process. I think we all know that while substantial numbers of people who have applied for refugee status are certainly bona fide, or consider there is a bona fide case to consider them in that way, others are not. People come and clog up the process. They come from countries from which there is absolutely no reason one could conceivably imagine that a person would seek to wish to become a refugee. The only reason the person might not wish to return to their native land would be because they had committed some criminal offence which would be equally criminal if committed on Canadian soil.
The former Government did not tackle, and the present Government has yet to tackle this particular problem. Yet it has come out with this particular Bill. I would like to say as well, Mr. Speaker, that there are other areas which I think are deserving of urgent consideration. One of these areas is the authority of the Immigration Appeal Board. I can say, Mr. Speaker, that the Appeal Board pronounces, and the law says that once it pronounces, the Minister should then act on the basis of that judgment, but there is nothing to enforce action by the Minister. In fact, there is a modest fine, but goodness knows how one could ever bring the Minister into court for a six-month sentence or a $1,000 fine for failing to live up to an order of the Immigration Appeal Board. There is no other enforcement mechanism.
I have had a case in my office for about three years, Mr. Speaker. It is the case of a man who is a productive citizen. He runs a restaurant in Ottawa. He has been seeking to bring his parents and, I believe, one or two young brothers and sisters into Canada from Pakistan over the course of a period of some two and a half years. They were refused entry into Canada. The immigration officer in Pakistan decided that he or she felt these people were not genuine, that they were going to leave the kids in Canada and go back to Pakistan.
The matter came up before the Immigration Appeal Board in January of this year. It was ruled upon in April, and in April the Immigration Appeal Board ordered that the appeal be allowed. In other words, it ruled that the immigration officer was wrong and that in fact the refusal to approve the application for landing was not in accordance with the law. This particular case illustrates the kind of problems which people in my Party who are helping immigrants and sponsors have been having. The family reunification program is blocked because there is not an adequate number of immigration officers in countries where people are looking for reunification, Pakistan being a notorious example, the Islamabad office being an office where there are particular problems.
One might almost say that there is discrimination built into administration because immigration offices are to be found in every major European country but in other countries, in Asia and in Africa, applicants must travel sometimes thousands of miles to find a Canadian office where they can put in their application.
In this particular case I wrote to the Minister in April and told him the Appeal Board had ruled and would he please see that this family was unified and would he expedite this matter. The Minister wrote back and acknowledged my letter and said he would let me know as soon as he had an answer. That was in April, Mr. Speaker, and I have been waiting for a response ever since. We have been in contact a dozen times with the Minister's office since then. It maintains that it has contacted the embassy in Islamabad on numerous occasions, but nothing has happened. Most recently, the people in this particular case were called to Islamabad and they expected to receive the medical forms to finish the procedure so that they could get on a plane and come to Canada. They went there and were told that new documents were needed about the kids' schooling
September 26, 1985

despite the fact that all the documentation which could conceivably be required had been handed in. They were not given the medical forms. Finally, I got on the telephone myself last week and said, "Will you please act. I am going to raise this matter in a week if I don't hear from you". I was told a telex would be sent to Islamabad. Many telexes have gone to Islamabad and it is like a black hole in terms of any action being taken. Unless the assistant in the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has responded since we came into the Chamber at two o'clock today, there has been no answer.
The individual called me the other day and told me he missed his family and said he wanted to go and talk to The Citizen. I told him to wait for a few days, that I had talked to the Ministry. This is the first immigration case I have been involved in with the Ministry in a year. I am slow to anger on these things, Mr. Speaker, but this is a case where, it seems to me, the Ministry itself mocks the authority of the Immigration Appeal Board. The Government then turns around with Bill C-55 and tells us, "By the way, the Immigration Appeal Board is not adequately staffed and, therefore, would you please allow us to increase the membership in the Board from 18 to 50 members?" We could increase the membership to 500 members, Mr. Speaker, but if the Ministry is not going to take the rulings of the Appeal board seriously, then we have real problems.
If the Appeal Board continues in its tradition of ignoring prima facie evidence on such matters as refugee claims, which was one of the factors which led to Rabbi Gunther Plaut to argue for a different tribunal in refugee cases, a tribunal which would be adequately informed, you could have 5,000 people on the Immigration Appeal Board and that would not be enough.
I see that the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is taking a very serious interest in some of the comments I am making. I appreciate his interest. I hope that Hon. Members on the Government side take this seriously. We are opposing this particular Bill, but it is clear that second reading will pass and the Government will have the authority to increase the numbers. The Hon. Member for Calgary West knows that our concern is that we do not know what kind of appeal tribunal we are going to have. We are going to have 35 new people on the Board who will have some expectation about their job. Jobs are hard to find these days and they would hope that they could keep that job. But they may be all Tories. They may well be the constituency assistants or the people who made up Marcel Masse's election expenses return. Who knows, Mr. Speaker. It could be any quality of person at all who could be appointed to that particular Board. Criteria are not laid down in this particular case and I think perhaps they should be. In fact, and I have not checked this with my colleagues, I would like to make a very serious suggestion to the Government. This is perhaps an individual's suggestion rather than a joint one. Hon. Members may be familiar with the tradition of magistrature in the United Kingdom. Magistrates there include a substantial number of citizens who do not have legal training; they are simply concerned with admin-
Immigration Act, 1976
istering the law. They are prepared, often on a voluntary basis, to serve in conjunction with a trained and full-time magistrate. We have some magistrates without legal training in Canada but they generally tend to work full-time. If there are backlog problems, and without pre-empting the decision surrounding the Plaut report, and perhaps as a precedent, we could amend this Bill so that two of the three members of these panels, rather than being appointed for two years, should be citizens with some competence and reputation in the community and who are prepared to give up time to sit in on a number of appeals. Some training courses could be given, but in many cases, whether they are refugee or sponsorship cases, we are not talking about a need for substantial training. We should not be making these decisions on the basis of legal technicalities or niceties. These decisions demand compassion, understanding and empathy. That is something that millions of Canadians have to offer. That might be a more productive way to work on the backlog, in addition to taking measures to reduce the potential backlog. I suggest that would allow us to tackle the backlog while leaving our options open with respect to early action on the Plaut report.
Both myself and my Party look forward to early action on that report, but for reasons I have given we have to say that we object to this particular measure. We think it is an inadequate beginning toward responding to a very serious problem.

She commended the Government for the provisions of this Bill and felt it would provide a solution to some of the problems.
You were not listening carefully. You were sleeping.
I was here.
You were sleeping. I heard you snoring.

The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was not even here. He must be omniscient; he knows what his colleague said.

If we hired enough officers to clear up the backlog, would that then take care of the flow of people coming into Canada and end that kind of

accusation of discrimination? I suggest that it would not. He said he just dealt with his first case. Mr. Speaker, first may I say that my colleague from Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) made it clear that while we support the measure in the Bill which permits landed immigrants to sponsor, we have grave reservations about the rest of the Bill. Instead of trying to elucidate every individual case he encountered, I would have preferred him to elaborate on the kind of amnesty he would like to see developed with respect to cases now pending, to settle the problems of specific groups.
1 wonder first of all, what criteria-if it is so arbitrary, what criteria he would apply to establish such groups or general amnesties? What we want to do in this legislation is increase the number of persons available to hear all these cases. And when we start judging the system itself... I think the hearings being conducted by the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration will help, and by the way, next Tuesday, we will be meeting Rabbi Plaut who is to explain part of it. Hearings have commenced on the subject.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised the Parliamentary Secretary is asking these questions, because it was his Department that was responsible for the fact that we now have about 15,000 refugees waiting to appear before the Immigration Appeal Board, pending decisions by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, which has legal status. After being heard by this committee, and we all know it hands down very few favourable decisions, refugees whose claims have been denied are entitled to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board, where the number of members has just been increased.
So as I said earlier, it is not a matter of amnesty but a matter of implementing special measures that were introduced in the past by Immigration Ministers, when it was the Department's practice or the Government's policy, when in fact decisions of the Immigration Appeal Board were unanimously or almost unanimously in favour of allowing refugees to remain in Canada.
For instance, does the Parliamentary Secretary maintain that we should force refugees from Poland, Hungary and other East European countries to go home? Is that going to be the position of this Government? Once these refugees arrive in Canada, do they really have a chance to go to other countries? Should we not act on what we see as our responsibility and allow these refugees to stay here? Is it the Government's position to accept them? Refugees from Europe or members of the Bahai sect, for instance are we really going to send them back to Iran? The answer is a definite no, because those refugees would not even survive if they were forced to go back to their own country.
So why are we asking these refugees to stay in the backlog with all the other refugees before they can appeal before the Immigration Appeal Board?
September 26, 1985

Briefly, instead of increasing our appeals capacity, we should be thinking of reducing the need for appeals. And that is what I and my party have proposed.

Mr. Speaker, I really do not mind if the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) refutes an argument of mine or even proves me to be wrong. I do not think I have to be afraid of that ever happening, given the way he argues, but if he succeeded I really would not mind too much. However, 1 wish he would quote me accurately. I would like him to tell me when I ever said that if the problem is big, or large, or overloaded, that we should do nothing about it.

With respect, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member said precisely that approximately eight minutes ago at the beginning of the period for questions and comments. He asked me if I thought that increasing the number of immigration officers or functionaries would in fact serve to master the flow of people applying for immigration in Canada. He was quite clearly suggesting that he did not believe that to be the case. He was, therefore, arguing that there was no point in doing anything at all to ensure that there are enough immigration officers to deal with the problems of immigration in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, and other countries where delays with regard to Canadian immigration authorities were notorious under the former Government and, regrettably, remain notorious under the present Government.

Mr. Speaker, I will begin my remarks today and, due to the timing of the House, will probably have to conclude on another day. It was my hope that this debate today might have been somewhat less partisan. This subject lends itself to much effort from all sides of the House to co-operate and come to resolution. As the chairman of the Standing Committee I would like to commend the degree to which that attitude has been present in the committee through 40 meetings.
The previous speaker invited the Government to act decisively and expressed concern about the fact that it had not done so. That is a very odd comment. I have been a member of the committee since I was first elected to the House of Commons in 1979. Aside from Main Estimates, that committee had not held a single meeting on the subject of immigration in the previous six years. During our first year we have had 40 meetings and three substantive reports. Bill C-55, which we are debating today, was brought forward within a very few months of our assumption of office. Any delay was due to the fact that there was a case before the courts and it behooved us to wait until that judgment was rendered before acting. We did not want to act in a manner that might have precluded desirable options. However, the case is over and the size of the backlog is known.
If the previous speaker had spent a little more time thinking, he would have recognized the wisdom of the chairman of the board in asserting to the committee that a two-year appoint-
Immigration Act, 1976
ment for a portion of those board members would be appropriate. The chairman laid out two reasons for this and they are still compelling. The chairman has considerable experience and in her judgment she will be able to get better quality board members. If we want fairness and sensitivity in that process we must consider the quality of the people who will commit themselves to participation in the process. The second reason is that the chairman and this piece of legislation bring forward a plan which would allow the backlog to be cleared up in three years. If that happens, we will not need as many members. This piece of legislation asserts that the Minister and the board be given the legal basis to expand the staff to clear the backlog, after which time the staff would be reduced.
On Thursday morning of this week the committee began its inquiry into the Plaut report. We heard evidence from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and representatives of the Sikh Federation of Canada. We will hear from two more sets of witnesses today at six o'clock. The basic message of the testimony heard was that the decision to be made as to whether someone either is not refugee, and is or is not entitled to the protection which this country can provide, is basically not an immigration question. Immigration has somewhat different characteristics.
Every Member in this Chamber knows that there are problems in the current immigration system. It is a shame that all 282 Members cannot sit on the committee and hear the testimony in order to understand the focus of the problem and learn what has to be changed. The committee is spending hours and hours on the task of understanding the immigration system. It is also spending hours and hours trying to understand how things can best be arranged to deal fairly with refugees. I ask the Members opposite to think seriously about that concept. I ask them to look at Thursday morning's transcript and ask themselves whether the issue of refugee determination in this country is essentially an immigration issue or an issue of a different kind. Clearly, there are immigration concerns which flow from the basic decision as to whether people are or are not entitled to the protection of this country because they are truly refugees.
To what extent should it be different? To what extent should it be run by a group of people with different training? Should the Immigration Appeal Board, which is the subject of the Bill before us, in reality be dealing with appeals from a refugee board? If we follow the basic outline of the Plaut report, we could improve upon it and bring forward an even better piece of legislation than he envisaged. Is it not possible to invent a system to deal with the determination of refugee status, involving different people, different training backgrounds and considerations other than those which guide the members who serve on the Immigration Appeal Board?
It seems to me that the impulse to block and delay this piece of legislation stems from a genuine and valid concern for the plight of refugees. However, the solution does not lie in changes to the make-up of the Immigration Appeal Board.

The solution lies in the Plaut report and the examination of that report by the committee. Then the Government would be in a position to bring forward the legislation required to create a better system. What do you think the Bill does?

The Bill will do something that is very human and very desirable. I am sure every Member of the House has heard representations from people who are stuck in the process. They do not wait one month, six months or one year; they wait years to have their situations regularized, to have a sense of confidence that they can purchase a home or take a long-term job. If we leave in existence a system which requires them to wait from two years to four years in a kind of legal limbo, we act in a cruel fashion toward people who are less able to protect themselves than most of us would be. I suggest that it would run against the traditions of Canada. Members of all Parties have met with the Minister. There is a willingness to modify this piece of legislation in committee if it can be improved in any way. In the interest of those people stuck in the system, their spouses and their children, I urge Hon. Members of the Liberal Party and of the NDP to reconsider the speed with which they are prepared to deal with the Bill. We have lost the months of July, August and September. We have kept everyone in the system in limbo for an additional 90 days. If it takes another month, it grows to 120 days, or if it takes another two months, an additional 150 days.
The only solution is to negotiate quickly. Let us move expeditiously, not recklessly. Let us not put a badly flawed piece of legislation in place. The committee has already spent four hours on first reading stage of the Bill. We attempted to pass it in the month of June. We almost succeeded, but not quite. The Minister is making another effort, as will the committee. However, it takes the will of the caucuses. That will exists in the Progressive Conservative caucus. I encourage Hon. Members listening to the debate today to see what they can do to create that will in their own caucuses. The faster we accomplish it, the better off many people will be.
I see that we are approaching the hour provided for Private Members' Business. I look forward to continuing the next time the Bill is before the House. However, I would be remiss if I did not pay tribute to the members of the standing committee. They laboured long and hard. I hope Hon. Members who have not had the opportunity to serve on that committee recently will consult with them about the existing situation and about the need to move as quickly as possible on this Bill, on the Plaut report and on a number of other issues.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION FOR PEACE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
SUGGESTED DEDUCTION FOR PEACE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of establishing a register of national and international organizations involved in peace research and education, and consider allowing residents of Canada who pay income tax to transfer a portion of their tax to one or more of these organizations, such amount to be calculated on the percentage of the national budget allocated to defence, which is currently 10.2 per cent.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to present the concept of the peace tax fund, as it has become known. This is the second time I have had an opportunity to present a motion similar to this one. I understand that the Government will probably oppose it again this time, as did the previous Government. I am sure, given enough time, the Government will change its mind about it and bring in legislation making these kinds of recommendations possible.
Given the serious situation facing the world today, 1 can only express the hope that the Government will change its mind soon. The urgency of the motion must be recognized by Hon. Members on all sides of the House. It urges two actions upon the Government. First, it urges the establishment of a register of national and international organizations involved in peace research and education. Second, it asks the Government to consider allowing Canadians to transfer that portion of their income tax which normally goes to defence to one or more of these organizations. We can call the process of establishing such a register and providing for the transfer of funds the establishment of a peace tax fund.
There are two basic reasons Hon. Members on all sides of the House should support my motion. The first one is a reason of principle and the second is a more pragmatic one. The House should recognize that the payment of taxes for military purposes is a question of conscience for many Canadians or a question to which they cannot agree. The Government should recognize that the establishment of a peace tax fund provides a helpful way in which to channel funds toward peace research and education, two areas which are sadly in need of more financing. In turn, I will comment on each of these reasons. Many Canadians object to the payment of taxes to support military activities because it is incompatible with their consciences. In many cases it is a matter of religious conviction. In other cases it is a matter of individual consciences telling them what is right and what is wrong. It is directly related to the question of conscientious objection to military service.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION FOR PEACE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
speechtext:
Order, please. It being 5.55 p.m., the House will now proceed with the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.
Let me read briefly from a letter written by a woman in my constituency, a letter she wrote to the former Minister of National Revenue. In it she said:
September 26, 1985

My question is this: Will the Government of Canada establish a Peace Tax Fund for those of us who, according to our consciences, cannot pay for war, or preparation for war? Under the Charter of Rights, being guaranteed Freedom of Conscience, I trust that the answer will be "yes". I do not intend to act against my conscience in order to accommodate any law that has been made by people without regard for conscientious objection.
This is quite unlike, having "a different opinion" as you suggested, about how tax money should be spent. There are many ways of spending taxes with which I disagree, but there is only one that is against my conscience, therefore, I must act according to its direction. My conscience clearly dictates that killing is wrong. I do not expect the Canadian Government to order me to pay for war-
Conscientious objection to participation in war or preparation for war has a long Canadian history going back at least to the time of the American Revolution. At that time Mennonites and Quakers, for reasons of conscience, had not participated in the war on either side. This non participation made them suspect to the Americans and, at the same time, made them desirable immigrant prospects for the colonial Government of Upper Canada. At that time, Lord Simcoe promised them exemption from military service and this was given legal recognition by the legislature of Upper Canada in the Militia Act of 1793. The Act provided that in return for exemptions on military service those who were exempted should have to pay an annual fee toward the cost of maintaining the militia.
Members of the Society of Friends or Quakers saw a direct link between support of the militia by paying money and actually serving in the militia. Most of them refused to pay that fee levied upon them even though the penalty included such things as seizure of personal property and prison terms. Both Quakers and Mennonites lobbied to have the fee removed, which finally happened in 1849. We had similar moves in 1873 to encourage immigration of a group of Russian Mennonites when an Order in Council granted:
Entire exemption from any military service ... to the denomination of Christians called Mennonites.
Between 1874 and 1880 over 8,000 Mennonites came from Russia to the Canadian Prairies.
In 1898 and 1899 similar Orders in Council were approved to encourage emigration of Doukhobors and Hutterites. We have this long tradition in Canada of the historic peace churches, the Society of Friends, the Mennonites, the Hutterites and the Doukhobors who have always objected to serving in the war. This has been linked in the past to making payments in lieu of that service.
During the First World War there was a great deal of pressure for universal conscription and there was a real struggle to maintain that principle of conscientious objection, but it was maintained. Similarly, in the Second World War. I want to urge upon all Members the importance of individuals acting on the basis of their own conscience. I know within our own caucus and I hope within other caucuses that this is one area where on a question of conscience individuals have the right to disagree publicly with their caucuses and to vote against their caucuses on questions of conscience. We have heard of war crimes, Mr. Speaker, where people have been condemned because they refuse to act on the basis of their conscience.
Income Tax
I would like to read some comments from the philosopher Thoreau in his famous essay "And the duty of civil disobedi-ance", written over 100 years ago. He wrote:
There are thousands who are in opinion opposed to slavery and to the war, who yet in effect do nothing to put an end to them; who,... sit down with their hands in their pockets, and say that they know not what to do, and do nothing; who even postpone the question of freedom to the question of-
Wait for it, Mr. Speaker-
-free trade, and quietly read the prices-current along with the latest advices from Mexico, after dinner, and, it may be, fall asleep over them both-They hesitate, and they regret, and sometimes they petition; but they do nothing in earnest and with effect. They will wait, well disposed, for others to remedy the evil, that they may no longer have it to regret. At most, they give only a cheap vote and a feeble countenance and Godspeed, to the right, as it goes by them.
Thoreau continues:
Cast your whole vote, not a strip of paper merely, but your whole influence. A minority is powerless while it conforms to the majority; it is not even a minority then; but it is irresistable when it clogs by its whole weight-If a thousand men were not to pay their tax-bills this year, that would not be a violent and bloody measure, as it would be to pay them, and enable the State to commit violence and shed innocent blood. This is, in fact, the definition of a peaceable revolution.
Today we see a shift from the emphasis on direct military service to the payment of taxes which support a huge military machine. One writer, Muriel Luca from Foremost, Alberta, said:
For more than 200 years Canada has allowed freedom of conscience in relation to military service. However, today's military service is overwhelmingly in the form of paying for the increasingly expensive new weapons, much to the satisfaction of the munitions makers. My hands are just as bloody from helping finance nuclear missiles as they would be personally running another human being with a sword.
It is that sense which leaves many people to declare that paying taxes that go to military purposes is against their military conscience. More than 250 people across Canada have already taken action and have taken that portion of their taxes which would normally go for military purposes and put it into a peace trust fund. They are organizing and urging the Government of Canada to legalize this procedure so they are able to do it with Government sanction.
They point to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in our new Constitution of 1982. I would like to read the first two articles of that Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It reads:
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:
(a) Freedom of conscience and religion-
Freedom of conscience, Mr. Speaker, is the first freedom to be guaranteed by our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. But what does freedom of conscience mean? So far Parliament has left it to the courts to interpret the meaning of what freedom of conscience means as well as what other sections of the Charter are going to mean. The peace trust people would like to see this clarified. The cost of taking a case to the Supreme Court is estimated at something like $255,000, over one-quarter of a million dollars, to have a question clarified.

September 26, 1985
Income Tax
I would like to quote from David Vickers, a former Attorney General of British Columbia, a very distinguished lawyer in B.C. He said:
The interpretation which courts will place on the first freedom, the freedom of conscience, is not really known. I suggest that if it's to mean anything, it must be a guarantee, not just to believe in something, but also to put those beliefs into action.
Freedom of conscience is not just to be able to maintain a private inward belief but to be able to act in accordance with your beliefs. Certainly when it comes to a basic question such as whether or not we are going to support the military, I think that has to be recognized. There is nothing in this motion that goes beyond what are the reasonable and just limits that any society can impose. Without waiting for a court decision I would urge the Government to make provisions so that freedom of conscience can be a reality for people instead of just nice words on a piece of paper.
The peace trust people have organized themselves into a charitable society known as Conscience Canada which is actively working to have the Government make those changes and I urge it to adopt the motion which I am presenting which would accomplish that. I urge this action to provide freedom of conscience at a practical level so that our Constitution is effective, rather than having to wait for the courts.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, there are pragmatic reasons why this motion should be adopted. The practical reason for supporting this Bill, even if there were no conscientious objectors, is that we need to provide money for peace research and for education. Already our world is spending far too much money on weapons of destruction. This has two effects. First of all it drains money from other projects. There is still a myth abroad that somehow military expenditures create jobs, but dollar for dollar it has been shown that this is not an efficient way of creating jobs. Military expenditures, dollar for dollar, are one of the most inefficient ways of creating employment. This is one area where there has to be some education of the public. This is one area where we want to see more research so that people and industries that are already engaged in military projects would be able to make the transition to more constructive forms of human endeavour.
Earlier this week the CBC had a program marking the fortieth anniversary of the United Nations. Just as an indication of how much arms budgets are spiralling out of control, the CBC reported that today the United States spends more money on military music than it does on its budget for the United Nations. Yet there continue to be some very well orchestrated complaints about the cost of the United Nations.
Canada has a military budget of $9.4 billion, more than four times the amount we allocate to international development which is $2.1 billion. We are spending four times as much money preparing for war as we are in trying to correct the basic human situation that leads to war. This whole scale of things is completely out of control. Regarding the peace tax, people say, let us vote with our money, let us put our money into peace education and research and try to redress that
balance. What is the Government afraid of? Why will it not agree to this kind of proposal?
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, world armaments threaten to destroy us all. The balance of terror is becoming badly unbalanced. The United States plans to spend $26 billion on star wars research and we are concerned about Canadian complicity in that. Even though the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has given an official "no" to that star wars research on the part of the Canadian Government, the door seems to be open for individual Canadian firms to participate. It reminds me of the old song "Your lips tell me no, no, but there is yes, yes in your eyes". Along with the "yes, yes", there are the dollar signs in the eyes of some Canadian manufacturers who hope to make a quick buck out of increasing the balance of nuclear terror in our world.
Our leaders raise the question of Canadian complicity in the making of nuclear bombs with the use of Canadian uranium. One year ago the Prime Minister spoke at the St. Francis Xavier University, September 28, 1984, and he said preservation of peace is "the central issue confronting our generation". But what has he done since then? Very little.
In conclusion, Mr Speaker, Canadians would like to see more positive leadership from the Government on the subject of peace. They would also like to contribute directly themselves. The peace tax fund would enable them to do so. It provides a sensible alternative to the madness of the arms race, an alternative that takes account of conscience. I urge the acceptance of this motion upon all Members of the House.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be speaking to this motion today. I know the Hon. Member who has brought this before the House today is a responsible and conscientious parliamentarian and his remarks in favour of the motion are made with the best of intentions, I am sure.
This motion has obviously been put forward so that this House can show its commitment to the pursuit of world peace and so that Canada can reinforce its position of leadership in the worldwide efforts for security from the dangers posed by the very existence of nuclear weapons.
Although I agree with the ultimate goal of this motion, world peace, there are enough problems with some of the implications that I hope this House will not send it on as a concrete proposal for legislation. I think every Member of this House will agree tht the people of Canada, indeed this Government, are seriously concerned about world peace and that they are anxious to take every opportunity to express this concern as a high priority.
The motion on the floor shares this goal. This motion if enacted as legislation would allow Canadian taxpayers to earmark a certain part of the taxes they pay for special purposes. This tax revenue would be committed toward the activities of a registered international organization involved in peace research and education. The funds that would go to this use would be the equivalent proportion of the tax dollar that
September 26, 1985

would have gone to Canada's defence spending, that is about 9.3 cents of every dollar for the 1984-1985 fiscal year. This is obviously neither responsible nor reasonable.
This year personal income taxes amounted to about S30 billion of the Government's total revenues. To put things in perspective, this motion would make Parliament surrender control of about $3 billion each year, or close to 3 per cent of this year's total expenditures.
My first reaction to this motion was that it implies there is a disagreement between the wishes of Parliament and those of the Canadian people. This contradicts the basic belief we all hold that says Parliament provides a forum where the different views and interests of Canadians can be engaged and debated. It is hoped that the result of this process will be policy and legislation that pursues the national interest in the most effective way possible.
If we accept the principle behind this motion we will have to admit that Parliament is not succeeding in its most basic goal. In the case of defence policy I think that our Government has taken particular care to see that its defence spending priorities reflect the appropriate balance between the need for an effective military capability and, yes, an earnest desire to enhance national and international security.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I think that this policy supports in a very deliberate way the traditional role that Canada has played in international affairs and that we have earned respect for, that is a role highlighting leadership in bringing about the peaceful resolution of conflicts around the world and voicing the importance of moderation and understanding in that relation between all nations.
Even more significantly, I think our Government's defence policy is an expression of the views and priorities of the Canadian public. The public has by and large supported the approach we have taken on questions relating to national defence and international security. Of course, there will always be debate over precisely the best way to achieve the goals we have set for ourselves of a nation, as part of North America and as members of the NATO Alliance. A difference of opinion is always healthy in the sense that it ensures that alternatives will be considered most carefully. This is particularly evident in the activities of the Canadian Institute for Arms Control and Disarmament. The establishment of this organization was a clear expression of the fact that the Government sees as important precisely the same objectives as the Hon. Member has brought forward in his Bill tonight.
The Government's recent decision with respect to the Strategic Defence Initiative was indicative of our appreciation for the democratic process. When concerns were raised over the merits of this proposal through the direct representation of Canadians, the media and the speeches of Members of this House, the Government took care to appeal to public participation in this decision. I believe that the final choice not to participate in SDI directly as a Government was very strongly influenced by a number of widely held reservations about this new strategy on the part of Canadians.
Income Tax
Defence policy is of such a crucial nature that the principles embraced by the Government, more so than in any other area of policy, must be sensitive to the prevailing attitudes among the electorate. At the same time, however, 1 think that this area of Government policy is most effectively dealt with by the parliamentary and Cabinet decision-making process.
I believe the views and opinions of Canadians must be considered in forming Canada's defence policy. This process, however, depends on the institution of Parliament. Parliamentarians have access to resources and information, they have opportunities for debate and discussion and they have a legislative process, all of which ensure that conclusions are reached responsibly and legitimately. Matters as sensitive and complex as defence policy rely very heavily on the testimony of experts and on healthy debate between those with widely differing views.
I am afraid that the motion being debated today would not satisfy the principles of parliamentary democracy that are the traditions of this House. To illustrate this point, I suggest that we imagine what it would be like if we could earmark our tax returns for any purpose that we might personally feel important. I am sure that this would result in a very colourful range of Government-sponsored activities. Although this would be a very clear expression of public preference, it would not be an improvement over our present arrangement. More importantly, this kind of tax provision would introduce total disorder into the duties of the House of Commons. Members of Parliament would cease to exercise their responsibilities and policy would not be the product of a deliberate and thoughtful process.
The final point I would like to make is the simplest of all. I disagree with this motion because I believe the restraints imposed by our huge deficit have made defence spending, not to mention spending on environmental protection, very inadequate. As a nation-state, Canada has to fulfil certain responsibilities, primarily to our own defence and secondly to the safety and security of our allies. In the context of other obligations and commitments, the Government has allocated certain funds for national defence. Still our forces rely on obsolete technology and deteriorating equipment. It is very questionable as to whether or not we could offer any defence whatsoever to our sovereign territory, no matter how much we cherish it. Unfortunately, we inherited this terrible state of defence from the previous administration.
As a member country in good standing in NATO which certainly enjoys benefits commensurate with our contributions, we must be careful to honour our obligations. Support for this motion would certainly bring into question our commitment to the goals of our alliance and indeed to the values of peace and security that we are trying to uphold so well.
Finally, significant reductions in nuclear armaments can only be achieved if they are verifiable. Negotiations have to be conducted from a position of credibility. 1 believe that support for this motion would seriously jeopardize this goal.
It is important for all Canadians to know that to protect the interests of our country, we must speak from a position of

September 26, 1985
Income Tax
strength, not weakness. For those naive enough to believe that this is not true, I would suggest that they talk to people from Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary or Afghanistan, to name just a few. The fate of these countries should serve as a constant reminder to us of the way Soviets can be trusted around a so-called negotiating table. Eternal vigilance will always be the price of freedom.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION FOR PEACE RESEARCH AND EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to take part in the debate and to discuss this proposal which, in my judgment, is a real challenge to the imagination. I say it is "a real challenge" because the sponsor of the motion, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), is challenging all of us to ask ourselves whether we are doing all we can and all that should be done to promote a peacekeeping effort all over the world.
He is also challenging us to consider the role of our defence forces and determine whether they do contribute to peacekeeping.
The motion is also very imaginative and its New Democratic Party sponsor has shown a remarkable spirit of innovation by drafting this altogether novel tax proposal.
I will try to prove in my remarks that, unfortunately, such imagination and innovation can be misleading, and that the rather novel tax structure described in the motion is very much like Pandora's box-full of unpleasant surprises for anyone who opens it.
Mr. Speaker, my Government colleagues have spoken or will eventually speak on some of the significant issues raised in this motion with respect to what is being done and what could be done to promote peace and security throughout the world.
For my part I intend to speak to the tax issues raised by the motion. I have nothing against openly supporting any legitimate effort to restore world peace, but I have serious reservations concerning the tax mechanism we should use to that end.
The wording of the motion would indicate that the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands has drawn his own conclusion, namely that maintaining defence forces does not promote peace. He would fund peace research and information organizations by using some of the tax revenues allocated to the defence budget. One must conclude that he considers that peace and defence activities do not go together, like oil and fire, and that anybody who is in favour of one kind of activities must necessarily be against the other kind.
Of course, the Hon. Member is entitled to his opinion. The rest of us are certainly entitled to have ours, different though they might be in this respect. I will show that the mechanism proposed in the motion would, in a way, leave very little choice to the taxpayers who happen to believe that maintaining our armed forces contributes to peacekeeping throughout the world. I say this because the way this tax deduction would work out we would be urging the taxpayer to hand some of his income taxes over to bona fide peace research organizations, and we would also be indicating quite clearly that the money should come from the defence budget.
It seems to me that by adopting the proposal we would be offering this kind of alternative to the taxpayer. I do not think it is a clear proposal in black and white, and that the good guys are all on one side and the bad guys on the other side. In my opinion, nothing in the income tax return should indicate that the taxpayer is either for or against defence spending and peacekeeping effort.
I am wondering why the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands did not draft his motion so as to use the traditional tax mechanism available to all Canadians who want to support public welfare organizations and who want to take advantage of tax incentives to do so. Of course, we all know this mechanism, the deduction for charitable donations. The definition of charitable organization under our tax system is wide ranging. We do not see any problem if peace research organizations were to be recognized as charitable organizations eligible for this deduction. We all know how the deduction works. If a taxpayer is assessed at a marginal rate, say 35 per cent, everytime he gives $1 to a charitable organization the public treasury, federal or provincial, contributes 35 cents, so the taxpayer's donation amounts in fact to 65 cents.
This tax deduction for charitable donations has a long and honourable history. It is almost as old as income tax and it is almost part of it. It is a simple procedure whereby the State acknowledges the fact that any society derives benefits from the work done by charitable organizations. We find it hard to understand why such a simple procedure is not enough to
September 26, 1985

achieve the objective of the sponsor of the motion under consideration today.
Enough of these idealistic musings. Let us get back to earth. Suppose we look at how this particular proposal would work out in practice. First of all, we must realize that this idealistic and very selective process of transferring tax revenues would have to be indicated on the personal income tax return, also known as the T-l form. Since it would be a reduction in tax payable, the amount would have to be indicated at the end of the return.
The taxpayer would have to be asked the following question: Do you wish to have your income tax reduced by 10.2 per cent, or whatever the percentage happened to be in that year, and have this portion transferred to the organizations involved in peace research and education as specified? I am not sure the sponsor of the motion provided any explanatory notes to indicate to the taxpayer what this particular percentage represents, in other words, the percentage of the federal budget directly allocated to defence.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of comments one could make on this kind of proposal. Indeed, it raises a number of questions in my own mind, and I hope in the minds of the other Members of this House. For instance, what strict assurance does this somewhat fanciful procedure provide that the Government's tax revenues are allocated correctly and efficiently? We believe there is no way to predict the exact percentage of tax revenues to be transferred.
I believe we could expect the peace organizations that would benefit from this procedure to launch an all-out advertising campaign, urging taxpayers to opt for such a method. And after all, the taxpayer would probably be very quick to conclude, as we all would, that it would not cost us a cent to make what could be called a pious choice. Of course, Mr. Speaker, if someone is asked: Are you in favour of peace? He will probably answer right away: Why yes. Obviously. And in the taxpayer's mind, he would be giving the Government's money and not his own.
It is quite conceivable that the transfer of tax revenues could be very significant. After all, almost everyone is in favour of peace, with the exception of a few bellicose individuals and those who benefit directly from war. The taxpayer could well be in favour of this concept, believing it would not cost him a penny. And he would probably not consider other aspects of a plan he would assume had received official recognition since it appears on the income tax return.
However, there are other aspects to be considered. For instance, what assurance do we have that the revenues thus transferred to peace organizations are well spent? Will they achieve the desired results? And if the transfer of $1 million to peace research and education achieves a certain level of results, would $10 million increase those results tenfold? Or is there a law of decreasing returns that applies to this area as well?
Income Tax
Mr. Speaker, these are some of the questions a responsible Government must ask when allocating its budget expenditures.
However, the problem with the proposal before the House this evening is that such questions would not be asked. The Government would have no control over the percentage of tax revenues thus allocated to these expenditures. The scope and effectiveness of advertising campaigns orchestrated by peace organizations would probably have a significant impact on that amount. We would therefore have a percentage somewhere between zero and 10.2 per cent of federal tax revenues that would escape the control of Government and Parliament.
I said a few moments ago that the taxpayer would tend to think this plan would not cost him a penny. He might be wrong. If this proposal were fully implemented, it would mean that some $4 million in tax revenues would be transferred from our personal income tax. Consequently, if the transferred amount is significant, the Government might well be obliged to increase taxes to fill the gap, unless Hon. Members are prepared to let the budget deficit increase over and above what it is now, which is out of the question, in terms of the Budget proposals formulated last May.
Supporters of this idea might maintain that the amount is relatively small, that peace is very important, and that it is worth setting aside the principles of appropriate control of public expenditures for the sake of a very noble cause. The argument is undoubtedly very seductive. But how far should we expand this principle? We would be opening the door very wide.
If we accept the transfer of tax revenues to peace research, would there be other causes we might have to accept as well? How far would we extend this new principle? For instance, Governments spend significant amounts of money on hospital care, health insurance and other kinds of public health plans. Would we accept a system under which the Canadian Medical Association could set up a private health care plan to which taxpayers could transfer a certain percentage of their tax payable?
There are Canadians who do not have children and who take a very sceptical view of the spending of public funds on education or daycare centres and the welfare and maintenance of families in general. Would we allow these Canadians to transfer another percentage of their income tax to an area closer to their interests or concerns? Would we then have as many mini-budgets as we have citizens in Canada?
I could give other examples, Mr. Speaker. The point 1 am trying to make is that the importance of peace research is not the issue here. We are dealing with a much more basic question, namely can Canadians shirk their social responsibilities as citizens? In our system of responsible democratic Government we use Governments to make certain decisions which benefit society as a whole. Oftentimes these are very difficult decisions to make, and now and again they are unpopular. But they are choices we cannot avoid

September 26, 1985
Income Tax
making. I would imagine that defence expenditures fall in the last category.
But making those decisions on behalf of society as a whole is the basic principle of a responsible democratic Government elected as such by the people. Any attempt to avoid making those decisions, or some of them anyway, flies in the face of the principle of responsible Government.
We are not trying to say that citizens should not be interested in knowing how their tax dollars are spent.
We wish more people would show that kind of interest: our democracy would be stronger for it. However we must make a distinction between defence-or the acceptable promotion of defence, or the condemnation of that defence, of certain categories of public expenditures-and the fact that we can decide not to finance a given Government project through certain tax mechanisms that may be simpler.
Given our democratic Government system, the rules must be the same for everybody. We are not talking about a selective Government for certain individuals, by certain individuals, and in the interest of certain individuals.
We are sure that the sponsor of the motion did not draft it with a view to upsetting the well estabished nature of our system of Government. No doubt he is sincerely trying to draw the attention of the House to the vital importance of organizations working at the praiseworthy promotion of world peace in our troubled society. However, the so-called practical procedure which he advocates to reach that goal runs directly counter to important if not basic principles of our taxation system that are based on the responsibility of a government elected by the people. 1 think that it is a vital point which deserves to be stated at this time and I am pleased to have had the opportunity to do so this evening.

I believe the Parliamentary Secretary made it clear what violation this motion would do to that principle. There is at present no provision in the Income Tax Act which allows individual taxpayers to determine the specific areas in which their taxes should be used. Any change in the allocation of personal taxes such as in the proposal would involve an amendment to the Income Tax Act. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is responsible for both originating and amending tax legislation. My colleagues on both sides of the House will be speaking on the taxation issues when the motions come up on the Budget motion debate.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, Canadians may receive tax exemptions on their contributions to non-profit Canadian peace organizations, as registered in publications such as the Mennonite Central Committee's, "A Directory of Canadian Peace Organizations with International Concerns". There are all kinds of organizations so listed. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you are aware of many of them. I submit that the Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party must be aware of them as well.
It is the belief of this Government that defence and peace activities are not mutually exclusive, but are, indeed, complementary. If I may put it this way, they are the two wings which allow the bird to fly. We must have defence capability or we will not have security, and therefore we will not have peace. Someone observed long ago that every country will have an army on their soil, either their own defence force or the defence force of someone else. I think that is a very important truth in today's troubled world. We try to keep a balance between maintaining the western alliance while taking every reasonable opportunity to advance the cause of arms control, disarmament, and general global peace and security. In other words, you cannot seek an arms control agreement unless you have some credible defence force.
I would now address the ways in which Canada is promoting peace and security at the present time which negate the need to finance peace research and educational organizations by diverting tax funds from defence expenditures.

Canada's security policy has rested on three complementary foundations for the past 35 years: Deterrence of conflict through the collective security arrangements in NATO and NORAD; pursuit of equitable and verifiable arms control agreements; and commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes, including collective efforts to resolve the underlying social, economic and political causes of international tension.
Our country and this Government recognize the need for collective efforts to deter agression against North America and Europe. We support and contribute to this defence effort. The Alliance will possess only minimum levels of armaments consistent with effective deterrence, while at the same time we will pursue dialogue and equitable balance and verifiable arms control agreements. Our object, of course, is stability and security for all people in the Alliance.
All Members know that our Alliance relies on a deterrent strategy which takes into account the reality of nuclear weapons. Deterrence, including conventional, intermediate range and strategic nuclear weapons must provide sufficient stability to enable us to negotiate international arms control agreements. Each NATO member must contribute to sharing the collective defence burden while benefiting from its protection. Our direct contributions to deterrence and defence lie in providing effective conventional forces. This is not a question of morality, it is a question of how we can best contribute to our own security given our limited resources for defence.
Our Government, I am proud to say, has made clear its intention to meet its obligations to the Allies within the scope of contributing to stability in East-West security matters. We have committed ourselves to sufficient defence spending to make our contribution effective and reduce the vulnerability of our forces in the field. In short, sir, an effective defence ensures peace better than anything else developed up until today.
It should be noted, however, that budgetary expenditures in the defence sector are manifested in a variety of non-military ways that are of direct benefit to all Canadians in the pursuit of peace in general. AGRICULTURE-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE TALKS. (B) STABILIZATION AND INSURANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 24, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) if the Government would be prepared to make a commitment that our price stabilization and support programs as well as our supply management programs such as marketing boards would not become bargaining chips in the Canada-U.S. free trade negotiations. Every Member of this House knows that the most stable parts of our agricultural industry today are those involved in the production of poultry, eggs, broilers, turkeys
and milk, as well as those commodities covered by the Canadian Wheat Board. They are perhaps more stable than those commodities which do not have the advantage of a marketing board.
In the Government's documents dealing with free trade there is this paragraph which is especially disturbing to myself and I believe to many Canadian farmers. It is stated the agricultural sector has been exempt from earlier free trade area agreements, including the European free trade agreement. There will undoubtedly be pressures from agricultural interests on both sides of the border to exclude the whole agricultural sector from the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement. However, it is by no means clear that this would be in Canada's interests. There may be productivity advantages to be gained by adjustments within agriculture as well as from accelerating the transfer of farmers out of agriculture.
That is the view of the Government, Mr. Speaker. It thinks if we do away with our marketing boards, crop insurance, grain stabilization and all the rest of our agricultural programs there will be greater productivity achieved and the Government will achieve its aim of accelerating the transfer of farmers out of agriculture. That seems to be the Government's attitude towards agriculture. I think all Canadians will be very concerned about this when they look at the situation between Canada and the U.S.
Approximately 22 per cent of Canadian farmers are in serious financial difficulty and are in danger of losing their farms. In the United States that figure is approximately 33 or 34 per cent. I maintain that much of the difference is due to the fact that we have a number of controlled commodities with administered prices. We also have stabilization programs provided by the federal and provincial governments and programs such as the Western Grain Stabilization Program. As well, we have marketing arrangements through the Canadian Wheat Board. Without those, I believe that another 9 or 10 per cent of our farmers would be in serious financial difficulty.
Is the Minister willing to exclude agricultural products as was done in the European Economic Community? They do have an agreement on agriculture, but it is separate. Unfortunately, the Minister was not prepared to make a commitment that these marketing systems and stabilization programs would be kept out of the bargaining with the United States. If they are put on the table, we know that they will be bargained away.
Many farm organizations, including the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, have expressed concern. An article in The Toronto Star of August 27 reads in part as follows:
Agriculture shouldn't be part of any free trade package negotiated between Canada and the U.S., an Ontario Federation of Agriculture delegation told a Legislature committee yesterday.
The federation brief argued that the U.S. would want to dismantle many Canadian farm programs such as marketing boards and price stabilization programs.
In return, federation president Harry Pelissero said, Canada would probably get very little.
September 26, 1985

It is interesting to note that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), who is from Ontario, is acting in direct opposition to the Ontario Federation. Likewise, a report by the Alberta Pool indicates that it is concerned that agricultural stabilization programs and marketing systems will become bargaining chips in the high stakes which the Government will be playing in the free trade negotiations with the President which the Prime Minister announced today in the House of Commons.
I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will see the danger of bargaining away these things which have been so essential in maintaining some of the most viable parts of our agricultural industry in Canada.

Without going so far as accusing my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Foster) of using a double standard in his representations, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am always a little surprised when I hear him support the stabilization programs which exist in Canada and attack the Government position as defined in Bill C-25, because they agreed, mostly, on the fact that we are calling for their elimination.
This afternoon, I am quite surprised to hear him say something which is in part contrary to what he has been saying for the past few months.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question posed by the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) on September 24 in regard to bilateral trade negotiations with the United States.
Agricultural trade with the United States is of vital importance, not only to the agri-food industry, but to the whole economy. The United States has been Canada's number one market for agricultural exports for the past two years. Last year, of our total agricultural exports of $10.3 billion, the U.S. market accounted for $2.2 billion. If grains and oil seeds are excluded, the role of the U.S. market becomes even more important, as everyone knows.
Last year more than half of our non-grain exports were sold in the U.S. Last year our exports to the United Stats increased by nearly 30 per cent over 1983, mainly because of the difference in the value of our currencies. At the same time, U.S. agricultural exports to Canada increased by 16 per cent, to a total of $3.6 billion. That is nearly 60 per cent of Canada's total agricultural imports.
I think it is worth while to repeat those figures-exports of $2.2 billion, imports of $3.6 billion and a deficit of $1.4 billion per year in our agricultural trade with the United States. With that kind of money involved, both Canada and the United States have an interest in avoiding trade disputes such as the one recently experienced in the hog sector. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has been working with his American counterpart to ensure an ongoing exchange of information on agricultural trade matters. Furthermore, both Ministers are
Adjournment Debate
taking steps to ensure a good flow of information between industry leaders on both sides of the border. We think that is most important.
The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) has heard the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) this afternoon regarding Canada-United States trade. Obviously it would be premature at this point to speculate what will happen down the road in respect of agricultural aspects of Canada-U.S. trade discussions. However, the Hon. Member can be assured that in any negotiations with the United States on agricultural matters, we will be consulting fully with the industry. We are only interested in a deal which is in the best interests of Canadian agriculture.
