CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-ACQUISITION OF CANNED TUNA. (B) ISSUANCE OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question this evening concerns one which 1 directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) in the House and it revolves around the tuna scandal.
It appears that some time ago a company packed some decomposing tuna, and some of that particular shipment of tuna was packed prior to the election. The company did not have much success in convincing Fisheries inspectors to pass the tuna, as they found it to be rancid, decomposing and unfit for human comsumption. Apparently the last Government was not too favourable on overriding its inspectors. After the last election a new Government was in power. I remember the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in an off record discussion on the campaign trail happened to say: "Yes, if I am in power, 1 will definitely have my nose in the trough, too, along with my friends". I am wondering whether there is a linkage between that statement and the events of the tuna scandal.
Once the Conservative Party was in power, some very influential people from Atlantic Canada began to telephone Ottawa-the Premier of New Brunswick, the Atlantic Chamber of Commerce and the New Brunswick Fish producers. Of course, the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) said in September that he had raised that matter, before he retracted the statement. It was a fairly significant problem.

September 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
At one point it was mentioned that only 2 per cent to 3 per cent of the production of the company was involved, although it was close to a million cans. When October rolled around and the great pressure had been put on, the then Minister of Fisheries went down to taste it for himself. He eventually said: "Yes, I tasted three cans and two of them weren't too bad". I presume the taste test led some kind of procedure by which a contract was granted to the company to supply the Department of National Defence with $103,000 worth of the product of this company.
In November, this material appears to have been delivered to 32 Canadian Forces bases. Upon opening the cans, the cooks and the people at the bases found that it was rancid, decomposing and unfit for human consumption. Things certainly moved forward from that point, to the Ministry of National Defence removing the product. It went to fisheries inspection labs in Burnaby and Halifax, and the Ottawa Forces Base sent it to the health laboratories here. They found that the product was contaminated. Although it would not kill you, it certainly was not something you would want to eat.
As I understand it, as things unfolded, the product was sent back to the company. The company designated a second order as a replacement order. Before that order could leave the plant, fisheries inspectors designated it as unfit for human consumption.
Were members of the Canadian Armed Forces used as guinea pigs in this situation? In addition, was there an arrangement between the influential voices in Atlantic Canada and the new powers in Ottawa?
Given the testimony we have had and the kinds of information given in this House, conflicting statements, retractions and questions raised previously as well as other very questionable practices that have gone on, including early campaign statements by the Prime Minister, the questions are certainly valid. It would be very useful if the Government would come clean and tell us how this order, $103,000 worth of tuna that turned out to be, as fisheries inspectors have said, rancid and decomposing and unfit for human consumption went to the Department of National Defence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-ACQUISITION OF CANNED TUNA. (B) ISSUANCE OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a fellow Member of Parliament from British Columbia I can certainly appreciate that occasionally we do have a rather colourful turn of phrase or that we are tempted occasionally to overstate a case, but 1 know the Hon. Member from Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) is often a reasonable Member. He likes to hear the facts and the details. I will give him a little bit of that, and as I do I know he will appreciate the situation, the difficulty, understand and be assured regarding his question.
Certainly the Department of National Defence did enter a contract with Ocean Maid Food Limited of St. Laurent, Quebec to supply canned tuna for the Canadian Armed Forces. There can be no doubt about that. The Hon. Member should also recognize that during the current fiscal year, 1985-86, the Department of National Defence is involved with some 40,000 contracts. In what is called national procurement where food items are included there are 25,000 contracts and one million line food items. The total value of national procurement is $1,135 billion. There are over 100,000 types of food items involved.
When the Minister this afternoon mentioned that he could not be expected to be directly involved with every contract undertaken by DND, this was an understatement, not an overstatement, especially in light of the facts 1 have just mentioned.
The Department of National Defence, like any other Government institution, has rigid and demanding quality standards for foodstuffs in order that we can be assured that our Armed Forces are eating the best and the highest quality of food that can be purchased here. It is not an unusual occurrence that food products which do not meet out high standards in the Department of National Defence are returned to be replaced by the supplier, which was the case in this instance.
